\begin{theorem}[the double dual is natural]\label{thm:bidualnat}
On the category $\mathbf{FinVect}_K$ of finite-dimensional vector spaces, evaluation
\[
\iota_V:V\longrightarrow V^{**},\qquad\iota_V(v)(\varphi)=\varphi(v),
\]
is a natural isomorphism from the identity functor to the functor $V\mapsto V^{**}$, $f\mapsto f^{**}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Yoneda's lemma]\label{thm:yoneda}
For an object $A$ and a functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$, evaluation at the identity gives a bijection
\[
\Phi:\operatorname{Nat}(h^A,F)\longrightarrow F(A),\qquad
\Phi(\alpha)=\alpha_A(\mathrm{id}_A).
\]
The transformation corresponding to $x\in F(A)$ has components
$\alpha^x_B(f)=F(f)(x)$ for every arrow $f:A\to B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}\label{def:functor}
A \emph{functor} $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ assigns an object $F(A)$ to every object $A$ and an arrow $F(f):F(A)\to F(B)$ to every arrow $f:A\to B$, subject to
\[
F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f),\qquad F(\mathrm{id}_A)=\mathrm{id}_{F(A)}.
\]
A \emph{contravariant functor} from $\mathcal C$ to $\mathcal D$ means a functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal D$. It sends $f:A\to B$ to $F(f):F(B)\to F(A)$, so
$F(g\circ f)=F(f)\circ F(g)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:nat}
For functors $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, a \emph{natural transformation} $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$ chooses an arrow $\eta_A:F(A)\to G(A)$ for every object $A$, with
\[
G(f)\circ\eta_A=\eta_B\circ F(f)\qquad(f:A\to B).
\]
Thus the square in Figure~\ref{fig:universal} commutes for every arrow $f$. The transformation is a \emph{natural isomorphism} if every $\eta_A$ is an isomorphism. In that case the inverses form a natural transformation $G\Rightarrow F$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:product}
A \emph{product} of $A,B$ is an object $P$ with arrows $p_A:P\to A$ and $p_B:P\to B$ such that, for every pair $f:X\to A$, $g:X\to B$, there is exactly one $h:X\to P$ with
\[
p_A\circ h=f,\qquad p_B\circ h=g.
\]
We write $P=A\times B$ and $h=(f,g)$. A \emph{coproduct} is the arrow-reversed construction: an object $A\sqcup B$ with maps $i_A:A\to A\sqcup B$ and $i_B:B\to A\sqcup B$ such that every $f:A\to X$, $g:B\to X$ factors uniquely as $f=h\circ i_A$, $g=h\circ i_B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:adjunction}
Functors $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ are \emph{adjoint}, written $F\dashv G$, if there are bijections
\[
\varphi_{A,B}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(F(A),B)
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,G(B))
\]
natural in both variables. Explicitly, for $a:A'\to A$, $b:B\to B'$ and $h:F(A)\to B$,
\[
\varphi_{A',B'}(b\circ h\circ F(a))
 =G(b)\circ\varphi_{A,B}(h)\circ a.
\]
We call $F$ the \emph{left adjoint} and $G$ the \emph{right adjoint}.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:categories}
The following choices all satisfy the two composition rules.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item In $\mathbf{Set}$ the objects are sets and the arrows are functions. In $\mathbf{Grp}$ they are groups and homomorphisms; in $\mathbf{Ab}$, abelian groups and homomorphisms. The categories $\mathbf{Ring}$ and $\mathbf{CRing}$ use rings with $1$ and maps preserving $1$, with commutativity required in the latter. The zero ring is allowed. In $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ the arrows are $R$-linear maps, and $\mathbf{Vect}_K$ is the case of vector spaces over a field $K$. In $\mathbf{Top}$ the arrows are continuous maps; in $\mathbf{Top}_*$ both spaces and maps have a chosen base point. In each case composition is ordinary composition of functions.
\item A partially ordered set $(P,\le)$ gives a category: there is one arrow $x\to y$ if $x\le y$, and no arrow otherwise. Reflexivity supplies identities. Transitivity supplies composition, and any two arrows with the same source and target are already equal.
\item A monoid $M$ gives a category with one object $\bullet$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\bullet,\bullet)=M$. Composition is the monoid multiplication. For a group every arrow in this category has an inverse.
\item The objects of $\mathbf{Mat}_K$ are $0,1,2,\ldots$. An arrow $n\to m$ is an $m\times n$ matrix, and composition is matrix multiplication. The object $n$ records a dimension, rather than a particular vector space. Nevertheless its arrows act as linear maps $K^n\to K^m$. This example shows that objects need not themselves be sets equipped with extra operations.
\item Reverse every arrow of $\mathcal C$ to obtain its \emph{opposite category} $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$. Its objects are unchanged and
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(B,A)$.
Composition is the old composition read in reverse order.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:functors}
Each construction below comes with its rule on arrows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item A \emph{forgetful functor} discards structure: $\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ forgets multiplication, $\mathbf{Ring}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ retains addition, and $\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$ forgets the topology. It leaves the underlying functions unchanged.
\item The \emph{abelianisation} of $G$ is $G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/G'$, where $G'$ is the subgroup generated by commutators $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ (Volume~3, Exercise~2.4). A homomorphism $f:G\to H$ sends each commutator to a commutator. It therefore induces $f^{\mathrm{ab}}:G^{\mathrm{ab}}\to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$, given by $gG'\mapsto f(g)H'$. The induced map of a composite is the composite of the induced maps.
\item For commutative rings, $R\mapsto R^\times$ and $R\mapsto\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ define functors to $\mathbf{Grp}$. Apply a ring map to a unit or to every matrix entry. Applying it to $MM^{-1}=I$ proves that the image matrix remains invertible.
\item The constructions $\pi_1:\mathbf{Top}_*\to\mathbf{Grp}$ and $H_n:\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ from Volume~9, Chapters~5 and~6 are functors. The identities for induced maps proved there, such as $H_n(g\circ f)=H_n(g)\circ H_n(f)$, are exactly the functor rules.
\item The dual $V^*=\operatorname{Hom}(V,K)$ gives a contravariant functor. A linear map $f:V\to W$ sends a form $\psi\in W^*$ to $f^*\psi=\psi\circ f\in V^*$. Indeed $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$.
\item Fix an object $A$. The functor $h^A=\operatorname{Hom}(A,-)$ sends an object $B$ to the set of arrows $A\to B$, and an arrow $g:B\to C$ to the function $f\mapsto g\circ f$. The contravariant functor $h_A=\operatorname{Hom}(-,A)$ sends $g:B\to C$ to $f\mapsto f\circ g$, from $\operatorname{Hom}(C,A)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(B,A)$.
\item Between poset categories, a functor is an order-preserving map. Between groups regarded as one-object categories, it is a group homomorphism: the composition rule says that it preserves multiplication.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Brouwer, functorially]\label{ex:brouwer}
Let $i:S^1\to D^2$ include the boundary circle into the closed disc. A \emph{retraction} would be a continuous map $r:D^2\to S^1$ satisfying $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_{S^1}$. Applying $H_1$ would give
\[
H_1(r)\circ H_1(i)=\mathrm{id}_{H_1(S^1)}.
\]
But Volume~9, Chapter~6 computes $H_1(D^2)=0$ and $H_1(S^1)\cong\Z$. Thus the left side factors through the zero group and is zero, whereas the right side is not zero. No such retraction exists. As in Volume~9, a continuous self-map of $D^2$ without a fixed point would give a retraction by extending the ray from the image through the original point to the boundary. Hence every continuous self-map of the disc has a fixed point.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:nattrans}
Two examples show how to check the square on elements.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The quotient maps $\pi_G:G\to G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ are natural. Regard abelianisation as a functor to $\mathbf{Grp}$ by including $\mathbf{Ab}$. For $f:G\to H$ and $g\in G$,
\[
f^{\mathrm{ab}}(\pi_G(g))=f(g)H'=\pi_H(f(g)).
\]
Both routes send an element to the same coset.
\item The determinants $\det_R:\mathrm{GL}_n(R)\to R^\times$ are natural in the commutative ring $R$. A ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to S$ satisfies $\det(\varphi(M))=\varphi(\det M)$: the determinant is a sum of signed products of entries, with integer coefficients, and $\varphi$ respects every operation in that sum.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}[the natural operations on groups]\label{ex:natops}
Suppose an operation $w_G:G\to G$ is assigned to every group and commutes with every homomorphism: $f(w_G(g))=w_H(f(g))$. The components need only be functions, not group homomorphisms. Such families are the transformations $U\Rightarrow U$ for the forgetful functor $U:\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$.

Evaluation at $1$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}(\Z,G)$ naturally with $U(G)$, so $U\cong h^{\Z}$. Yoneda therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{Nat}(U,U)\cong\operatorname{Nat}(h^{\Z},U)\cong U(\Z)=\Z.
\]
For the integer $n$, the corresponding operation sends $g=f(1)$ to $f(n)=g^n$. These powers, including the constant identity operation for $n=0$ and inversion for $n=-1$, exhaust the possibilities. A proposed operation defined for every group can be tested on one generator of $\Z$. Exercise~\ref{ex:words} makes the same test with two generators.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:adjunctions}
These familiar constructions provide adjunctions.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The free-module functor $S\mapsto R^{(S)}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor $U:R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}\to\mathbf{Set}$. The bijection restricts a linear map to the basis $S$. Conversely, a function on $S$ extends by finite linear combinations. The free-group functor of Volume~9, Chapter~5 and the free commutative ring $S\mapsto\Z[X_s:s\in S]$ obey the same rule.
\item Abelianisation is left adjoint to the inclusion $\mathbf{Ab}\to\mathbf{Grp}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:abuniv} supplies the bijection $\bar f\mapsto\bar f\circ\pi_G$ between homomorphisms $G^{\mathrm{ab}}\to A$ and $G\to A$.
\item Fix a set $B$ and write $C^B$ for the set of functions $B\to C$. A function $h:A\times B\to C$ corresponds to $a\mapsto(b\mapsto h(a,b))$, a function $A\to C^B$. Evaluation, $(a,b)\mapsto k(a)(b)$, reverses this correspondence. Therefore $-\times B\dashv(-)^B$. This rearrangement of a two-variable function is called \emph{currying}, after Haskell Curry. It also works for empty sets: the unique empty function accounts for the boundary cases.
\item Giving a set the discrete topology is left adjoint to forgetting a topology, since every function from a discrete space is continuous. Giving it the indiscrete topology is right adjoint to forgetting, since every function into an indiscrete space is continuous.
\item For posets an adjunction is the equivalence $F(x)\le y\iff x\le G(y)$. For a finite Galois extension $L/K$ with group $\Gamma$, take the subgroup poset and the opposite of the intermediate-field poset. The maps $H\mapsto L^H$ and $E\mapsto\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)$ satisfy
\[
E\subseteq L^H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\subseteq\operatorname{Gal}(L/E).
\]
Both assertions say that every element of $H$ fixes every element of $E$. This is the Galois connection behind the terminology. The fundamental theorem of Galois theory (Volume~3, Chapter~10) says that in this finite Galois case the correspondence is an equivalence of these posets.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch01-subsets}
For a function $f:X\to Y$, let $\mathcal P(X),\mathcal P(Y)$ be the power sets ordered by inclusion. For $S\subseteq X$ and $T\subseteq Y$ define
\[
f_!(S)=f(S),\qquad f^{-1}(T)=\{x:f(x)\in T\},\qquad
f_*(S)=\{y:f^{-1}(\{y\})\subseteq S\}.
\]
Prove the two adjunctions $f_!\dashv f^{-1}\dashv f_*$. Use them to predict which maps preserve intersections or unions, then check those predictions directly, including empty intersections and empty unions. Explain why a point with empty fibre belongs to $f_*(\varnothing)$.
\end{exercise}

\begin{solution}{ex:leftadj}
\idea Opposite categories turn outgoing universal maps into incoming ones.
\writeup (a) The inverse adjunction bijections can be written
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}(G(B),A)
 \cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D^{\mathrm{op}}}(B,F(A)).
\]
They are natural, so $G^{\mathrm{op}}\dashv F^{\mathrm{op}}$. The functor $F^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a right adjoint and preserves products by Theorem~\ref{thm:rapl}. A product in an opposite category is a coproduct in the original one, giving the assertion with its induced injections.

(b) The free-module functor is left adjoint to forgetting. Since $S\sqcup T$ is the coproduct of sets, its free module is the coproduct of $R^{(S)}$ and $R^{(T)}$. Explicitly a finitely supported function on the disjoint union restricts to one on each summand. Conversely the two functions combine on their disjoint supports. For sets, currying gives $A\times-\dashv(-)^A$, after swapping the factors. The resulting coproduct isomorphism sends $(a,b)$ to the $B$ summand and $(a,c)$ to the $C$ summand, preserving the tags distinguishing the two summands.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:f2plane}
\idea Over $\mathbb F_2$, the kernel specifies a nonzero form on a plane completely.
\writeup (a) For nonzero $v$, the function $\eta_V(v)$ is zero on $\{0,v\}$ and one on the other two vectors. Choose $w$ independent of $v$. In the basis $(v,w)$, this is the second coordinate function, so it is linear. Also $\eta_V(0)=0$. Distinct nonzero vectors span distinct lines, hence give forms with distinct kernels. The map $\eta_V$ therefore bijects the three nonzero vectors with the three nonzero forms.

To check linearity in $v$, take distinct nonzero $v_1,v_2$. The form $\eta(v_1)+\eta(v_2)$ is nonzero, since its value at $v_1$ is $1$. Its value at $v_1+v_2$ is $1+1=0$. It is therefore the unique nonzero form vanishing on that vector, namely $\eta(v_1+v_2)$. If one vector is zero the identity is immediate; if they are equal, both sides are zero. Additivity implies $\mathbb F_2$-linearity. An isomorphism $f:V\to W$ preserves linear independence, so for every $v,w$,
\[
\eta_W(f(v))(f(w))=\eta_V(v)(w).
\]
This is precisely $f^*\eta_Wf=\eta_V$.

(b) The scalar argument required a nonzero $\lambda$ with $\lambda^2\ne1$. The only nonzero scalar in $\mathbb F_2$ is $1$, so it gives no contradiction. The example concerns planes and isomorphisms only. It does not provide a natural self-duality for all dimensions or for all linear maps.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch01-adjunction-order}
\idea An integer lies below a ceiling exactly when it lies below the original number.
\writeup (a) Both maps preserve order, since $d>0$. For integers $n,k$,
\[
F(n)\le k\iff n/d\le k\iff n\le dk=G(k).
\]
The first equivalence holds for negative $n$ too, by the definition of the least integer above $n/d$. Thus $F\dashv G$. If $d>1$, $G(1)\le1$ is false whereas $1\le F(1)=1$ is true, so $G\dashv F$ fails.

(b) Arrows follow the ordinary order, so a product is $\min(a,b)$ and a coproduct is $\max(a,b)$. Multiplication by the positive integer $d$ commutes with minimum. The increasing map $F$ commutes with maximum: if $a\le b$, both sides of $F(\max(a,b))=\max(F(a),F(b))$ equal $F(b)$. This verifies the two preservation claims without an abstract argument.

(c) With divisibility instead, common sources are common divisors and common targets are common multiples, giving gcd and lcm. An arrow means a different relation, so even the same underlying objects need not have the same universal constructions.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch01-subsets}
\idea Existential and universal conditions on fibres are the two adjoints to inverse image.
\writeup For $S\subseteq X,T\subseteq Y$,
\[
f(S)\subseteq T\iff S\subseteq f^{-1}(T),
\qquad
f^{-1}(T)\subseteq S\iff T\subseteq f_*(S).
\]
The first equivalence says that every $x\in S$ has $f(x)\in T$. The second says that for every $y\in T$, all points mapping to $y$ belong to $S$. These prove the two adjunctions.

Products in power-set orders are intersections and coproducts are unions. Right adjoints preserve intersections; left adjoints preserve unions. For arbitrary indexed families, direct checking gives
\[
f_!\Bigl(\bigcup_iS_i\Bigr)=\bigcup_i f_!(S_i),\qquad
f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_iT_i\Bigr)=\bigcup_i f^{-1}(T_i),
\]
\[
f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_iT_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_i f^{-1}(T_i),\qquad
f_*\Bigl(\bigcap_iS_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_i f_*(S_i).
\]
For example, a fibre is contained in every $S_i$ exactly when it is contained in their intersection. With no sets in the family, the union is empty and the intersection is the entire ambient set. The four identities still hold: $f_!(\varnothing)=\varnothing$, $f^{-1}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$, $f^{-1}(Y)=X$, $f_*(X)=Y$. Finally an empty fibre is contained in $\varnothing$, so every point outside $f(X)$ belongs to $f_*(\varnothing)$. This is required by the universal condition, rather than an exception to it.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch01-pullback}
\idea A compatible pair of maps already gives the only possible map to the subset of pairs.
\writeup (a) Define $h(x)=(u(x),v(x))$. The identity $fu=gv$ ensures $h(x)\in P$. Its projections are $u,v$. Any map with those projections has that ordered pair as its value at every $x$, proving uniqueness.

(b) The identity pair belongs to $P$. If $(a,b),(a',b')\in P$, then $f(aa')=f(a)f(a')=g(b)g(b')=g(bb')$, so the product is in $P$; inverses satisfy the same equality. Thus $P$ is a subgroup of $A\times B$. Its projections are homomorphisms. If $u,v$ are homomorphisms, the formula for $h$ respects multiplication componentwise, so the same existence and uniqueness proof works in $\mathbf{Grp}$.

(c) Here $P$ is the group of same-parity pairs $(a,b)$. Each such pair is uniquely
\[
(a,b)=a(1,1)+\frac{b-a}{2}(0,2).
\]
Consequently $(1,1),(0,2)$ is a basis and $P\cong\Z^2$ as an abstract group. It is a proper subgroup of the cartesian product, since $(0,1)$ is absent. With its specified projections it is therefore not the product of $\Z$ with itself: the pair of maps taking $1$ to $0$ and $1$ would require a lift with value $(0,1)$. The distinction is between an abstract isomorphism of objects and an isomorphism preserving the structural maps.
\end{solution}

theorem:
\begin{theorem}[Strassen, 1969]\label{linear:thm:strassen}
The matrix multiplication tensor satisfies $R_K(\langle2,2,2\rangle)\le7$. More explicitly, the following formulas multiply $2\times2$ matrices over any ring, even a noncommutative ring:
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_1&=(a_{11}+a_{22})(b_{11}+b_{22}),&M_5&=(a_{11}+a_{12})b_{22},\\
M_2&=(a_{21}+a_{22})b_{11},&M_6&=(a_{21}-a_{11})(b_{11}+b_{12}),\\
M_3&=a_{11}(b_{12}-b_{22}),&M_7&=(a_{12}-a_{22})(b_{21}+b_{22}),\\
M_4&=a_{22}(b_{21}-b_{11}),
\end{aligned}
\]
followed by
\[
AB=\begin{pmatrix}
M_1+M_4-M_5+M_7&M_3+M_5\\
M_2+M_4&M_1-M_2+M_3+M_6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Schmidt decomposition]\label{linear:thm:schmidt}
Every $\psi\in\C^m\otimes\C^n$ has a decomposition
\[
\psi=\sum_{s=1}^r\sigma_s a_s\otimes b_s,
\]
where $(a_s)$ and $(b_s)$ are orthonormal families in the respective factors and $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$. The coefficients are the nonzero singular values of $\Psi=(\psi_{ij})$, $r=\operatorname{rank}\Psi$, and
$\sum_s\sigma_s^2=\|\psi\|^2$. The zero tensor has the empty decomposition. For a unit vector $\psi$, being a product state is equivalent to $r=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[rules of the Kronecker product]\label{linear:prop:kronecker}
For matrices with the indicated operations defined, the following rules hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item The \emph{mixed product rule} is $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=AC\otimes BD$.
\item Adjoints and inverses satisfy $(A\otimes B)^*=A^*\otimes B^*$ and, for invertible factors, $(A\otimes B)^{-1}=A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1}$.
\item If square matrices $A\in M_m(\C)$ and $B\in M_p(\C)$ have eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ and $\mu_k$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, then $A\otimes B$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i\mu_k$. The matrix $A\otimes I_p+I_m\otimes B$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i+\mu_k$.
\item For these square matrices,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{tr}A\operatorname{tr}B,
\qquad
\det(A\otimes B)=(\det A)^p(\det B)^m.
\]
For rectangular matrices as well,
$\operatorname{rank}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{rank}A\operatorname{rank}B$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
definition:
\begin{definition}\label{linear:def:kronecker}
For $A\in M_{m,n}(\C)$ and $B\in M_{p,q}(\C)$, their \emph{Kronecker product} is the $mp\times nq$ matrix
\[
A\otimes B=
\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}B&\cdots&a_{1n}B\\\vdots&&\vdots\\a_{m1}B&\cdots&a_{mn}B\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The row indices are pairs $(i,k)$ and the column indices pairs $(j,l)$, in lexicographic order; the corresponding entry is $a_{ij}b_{kl}$. For column vectors this gives $(u\otimes v)_{(i,k)}=u_iv_k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{linear:def:tensorrank}
The \emph{tensor rank} $R_K(T)$ is the smallest nonnegative integer $r$ for which
\[
T=\sum_{s=1}^r u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s
\]
with all vectors over $K$. The empty sum is allowed, so only the zero tensor has rank zero.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}[grids and cubes]\label{linear:exa:grid}
The \emph{Cartesian product} of graphs $G\mathbin\square H$ has vertices $(g,h)$. Two vertices are adjacent when exactly one coordinate moves along an edge and the other stays fixed. Its adjacency matrix is therefore
$A_G\otimes I+I\otimes A_H$. By the preceding proposition its eigenvalues are $\lambda_i(G)+\lambda_k(H)$.

For a grid $P_m\mathbin\square P_n$, use the path eigenvalues of Volume~8, Exercise~3.3 to obtain
\[
2\cos\frac{\pi i}{m+1}+2\cos\frac{\pi k}{n+1},
\qquad 1\le i\le m,\quad1\le k\le n.
\]
For the hypercube $Q_n$, each coordinate is a copy of $K_2$, whose eigenvalues are $1,-1$. Adding one choice from each coordinate gives $n-2t$ with multiplicity $\binom nt$. This agrees with the character calculation in Volume~8, Exercise~5.1. The same separation of coordinates will give the grid Laplacian in Exercise~\ref{linear:ex:gridlap}.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[the rank depends on the field]\label{linear:exa:rotation}
Take slices $A=I$ and $B=J=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. The matrix $A^{-1}B=J$ has eigenvalues $i,-i$. It is diagonalisable over $\C$ and not over $\R$. The slice test and invertibility of $A$ give $R_\C(T)=2$ and $R_\R(T)\ge3$. The following real decomposition gives the matching upper bound:
\[
T=(1,1)\otimes(0,1)\otimes(1,0)
 +(-1,1)\otimes(1,0)\otimes(0,1)
 +(1,0)\otimes(1,-1)\otimes(1,1).
\]
For its first slice, add $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ to get $I$. For its second, add $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ to get $J$. Thus $R_\R(T)=3$. Matrix rank cannot change under extension of the field, because its nonzero minors are unchanged. Tensor rank can. Exercise~\ref{linear:ex:complexmult} finds the same obstruction in complex multiplication viewed over $\R$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[rank is not semicontinuous]\label{linear:exa:wtensor}
Let
\[
W=e_1\otimes e_1\otimes e_2+e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_1.
\]
Its slices are $A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, so
$A^{-1}B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. This nonzero nilpotent matrix is not diagonalisable: a diagonal nilpotent matrix would be zero. Thus the slice test gives $R_K(W)>2$, while the displayed three-term sum gives $R_K(W)=3$.

Over $\R$ or $\C$, for $\varepsilon\ne0$ set
\[
W_\varepsilon=\frac{(e_1+\varepsilon e_2)^{\otimes3}-e_1^{\otimes3}}{\varepsilon}.
\]
This is a sum of two pure tensors. Expanding its eight entries gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_\varepsilon=W+\varepsilon(&e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2
 +e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_2
 +e_2\otimes e_2\otimes e_1)\\
 &+\varepsilon^2 e_2^{\otimes3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence $W_\varepsilon\to W$ although $R_K(W_\varepsilon)\le2<R_K(W)$. Figure~\ref{linear:fig:wtensor} displays the three nonzero entries of $W$. In quantum terminology, its normalised version is the W state of three qubits.
\end{example}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:kroncommute}
\idea Swap the order of the two coordinate indices.
\writeup Define $P$ by $P(e_i\otimes e_k)=e_k\otimes e_i$. It permutes a basis and is therefore a permutation matrix, with inverse $P^{\mathsf T}$. Linearity gives $P(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$. Hence
\[
P(A\otimes B)(x\otimes y)=By\otimes Ax
 =(B\otimes A)P(x\otimes y).
\]
Pure coordinate tensors span, so $P(A\otimes B)=(B\otimes A)P$. Multiplying on the right by $P^{\mathsf T}$ gives the required similarity, and similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial and all eigenvalue multiplicities.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:kronnormal}
\idea Product identities pass to Kronecker products.
\writeup If the factors are normal, then
\[
(A\otimes B)(A\otimes B)^*=AA^*\otimes BB^*
 =A^*A\otimes B^*B=(A\otimes B)^*(A\otimes B).
\]
For unitary factors, both products are $I\otimes I=I$. For Hermitian factors, the adjoint identity gives Hermitian symmetry of the product. If they are also positive definite, their eigenvalues $\lambda_i,\mu_k$ are positive, so every eigenvalue $\lambda_i\mu_k$ of the product is positive. The spectral theorem then makes the product positive definite.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:strassencount}
\idea Solve the recurrence exactly, then compare signs along all powers of two.
\writeup Put $t_s=T(2^s)$. The operation count gives $t_s=7t_{s-1}+18\cdot4^{s-1}$, with $t_0=1$. Direct substitution shows that $t_s=7\cdot7^s-6\cdot4^s$ has this initial value and satisfies this recurrence, so induction proves it for all $s\ge0$. Consequently $T(n)=7n^{\log_27}-6n^2$.

Schoolbook multiplication has $n^3$ scalar products and $n^2(n-1)$ scalar additions, hence $2n^3-n^2$. Subtracting Strassen's count at $n=2^s$ gives
\[
D_s=2\cdot8^s+5\cdot4^s-7\cdot7^s.
\]
At $s=0$ the counts agree. Direct evaluation gives $D_1=-13$, $D_2=-135$, $D_9=-12\,729\,073$, and $D_{10}=175\,399\,785$. The last two signs correspond to rounded costs $2.81\cdot10^8$ against $2.68\cdot10^8$ at $n=512$, and $1.97\cdot10^9$ against $2.15\cdot10^9$ at $n=1024$.

To show that every later power also benefits, divide by $7^s$ and put $q_s=2(8/7)^s+5(4/7)^s-7$. Its difference is
\[
q_{s+1}-q_s=\frac{2}{7}(8/7)^s-\frac{15}{7}(4/7)^s
 =\frac{(4/7)^s}{7}(2^{s+1}-15)>0\quad(s\ge3).
\]
Thus $q_s$ is strictly increasing from $s=3$ onwards. Since $q_9<0$, monotonicity gives $q_s<0$ for $3\le s\le9$; the direct checks cover $s=1,2$. Since $q_{10}>0$, every $s\ge10$ gives $q_s>0$. Thus the first persistent improvement is $n=1024$. This count concerns full recursion to scalars; stopping at a block size and using an ordinary algorithm there changes the practical crossover.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:complexmult}
\idea The slice quotient detects the real obstruction, and two complex evaluation forms give the complex algorithm.
\writeup With slices $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, the quotient is
$A^{-1}B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. It has eigenvalues $i,-i$ and is not diagonalisable over $\R$, so real rank is at least three. The three real products in the text give the reverse bound.

Over $\C$, write $z_+=a+ib$, $z_-=a-ib$, $w_+=c+id$, $w_-=c-id$. These are algebraic linear forms in the coordinates, even when $a,b,c,d$ are themselves complex; the minus form is not then necessarily the complex conjugate of the plus form. The two products give
\[
ac-bd=\tfrac12(z_+w_++z_-w_-),\qquad
ad+bc=\tfrac1{2i}(z_+w_+-z_-w_-).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T=(1,i)\otimes(1,i)\otimes\tfrac12(1,-i)
 +(1,-i)\otimes(1,-i)\otimes\tfrac12(1,i).
\]
This has length two. The invertible first slice rules out rank one, so complex rank is exactly two.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:noapprox}
\idea A missing limit point gives an unattained infimum, and pure-tensor norms show the cancellation.
\writeup If $\|W-S\|=0$, then $S=W$, of rank three. Thus every rank-at-most-two $S$ has strictly positive distance from $W$. But $W_\varepsilon$ has rank at most two and tends to $W$, so the infimum of those distances is zero and cannot be attained.

For positive real $\varepsilon$, multiplicativity of the Frobenius norm on pure tensors gives
\[
\left\|\varepsilon^{-1}(e_1+\varepsilon e_2)^{\otimes3}\right\|
 =\frac{(1+\varepsilon^2)^{3/2}}{\varepsilon},\qquad
\left\|-\varepsilon^{-1}e_1^{\otimes3}\right\|=\frac1\varepsilon.
\]
The two norms are not exactly equal, but both tend to infinity. The sum tends to $W$ and therefore its norm tends to $\sqrt3$. In fact the orthogonal coordinate expansion gives $\|W_\varepsilon\|^2=3+3\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4$, making its boundedness explicit.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:schmidtcheck}
\idea Diagonalise the real symmetric coefficient matrix, then absorb its negative sign into one tensor factor.
\writeup Put $\lambda_\pm=(1\pm\sqrt{17})/2$ and
\[
u_\pm=\frac{(\lambda_\pm,2)^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{\lambda_\pm^2+4}}.
\]
They are unit eigenvectors of $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_\pm$. They are orthogonal because $\lambda_+\lambda_-+4=-4+4=0$. Since $\lambda_+>0>\lambda_-$, a Schmidt decomposition is
\[
\psi=\frac{1+\sqrt{17}}6\,u_+\otimes u_+
 +\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}6\,u_-\otimes(-u_-).
\]
Thus $\sigma_1\approx0.854$, $\sigma_2\approx0.521$. Their squared sum is one, either by the displayed formula or by $\|\psi\|^2=(1+4+4)/9=1$. The entropy is
\[
-\sigma_1^2\log_2\sigma_1^2-\sigma_2^2\log_2\sigma_2^2\approx0.843\text{ bits}.
\]
Both coefficients are nonzero, so the matrix has rank two and the state is entangled.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{linear:ex:gridlap}
\idea The independent coordinate directions add their eigenvalues.
\writeup The eigenvalues of $L_k=2I-A_{P_k}$ are $2-2\cos(\pi j/(k+1))$, $1\le j\le k$. Hence the eigenvalues of the grid matrix are
\[
\lambda_{ij}=4-2\cos\frac{\pi i}{m+1}-2\cos\frac{\pi j}{n+1},
\quad1\le i\le m,\quad1\le j\le n.
\]
They are positive, and the real symmetric matrix is positive definite. Write $c_m=\cos(\pi/(m+1))$, $c_n=\cos(\pi/(n+1))$. The cosine decreases along each index range. Its extreme negative endpoint is $-c_m$ or $-c_n$, respectively. Thus
\[
\kappa_2(L)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}
 =\frac{4+2c_m+2c_n}{4-2c_m-2c_n}.
\]
For $m=n$, $\lambda_{\min}=4-4\cos(\pi/(n+1))=8\sin^2(\pi/(2(n+1)))\sim2\pi^2/n^2$, whereas $\lambda_{\max}\to8$. Therefore $\kappa_2(L)\sim4n^2/\pi^2$. At $m=n=1$, the ratio is one, consistent with the one-entry matrix $(4)$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch02-sylvester-obstruction}
\idea A common eigenvalue leaves one scalar equation with zero coefficient.
\writeup The four scalar equations are $-x_{11}=c_{11}$, $-2x_{12}=c_{12}$, $0=c_{21}$ and $-x_{22}=c_{22}$. Thus a solution exists exactly when $c_{21}=0$. All solutions then are
\[
X=\begin{pmatrix}-c_{11}&-c_{12}/2\\t&-c_{22}\end{pmatrix},\qquad t\in\C.
\]
The block shear from Exercise~\ref{linear:ex:roth} removes $C$, so similarity follows even though the spectra overlap.

If $c_{21}\ne0$, examine an eigenvector $(u,v)$ of the upper block triangular matrix at eigenvalue $2$. The lower equation gives $v=(v_1,0)$, while the second coordinate of $(A-2I)u+Cv=0$ gives $c_{21}v_1=0$. Hence $v_1=0$ and $v=0$; then $u_1=0$, leaving only the free coordinate $u_2$. This eigenspace has dimension one. The block diagonal matrix has dimension two at eigenvalue $2$, one from each block. Similarity preserves eigenspace dimensions, so these matrices cannot be similar.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch02-quadratic-algebra}
\idea Whether $u^2-t$ splits with distinct real roots determines whether two evaluation products suffice.
\writeup The product is
\[
(a+bu)(c+du)=(ac+tbd)+(ad+bc)u.
\]
Three products always suffice: use $P=ac$, $Q=bd$, $R=(a+b)(c+d)$ and output $(P+tQ)+(R-P-Q)u$.

For $t\ne0$, the first slice $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)$ is invertible and the second is $B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. The quotient has characteristic polynomial $X^2-1/t$. If $t>0$, it has distinct real roots; the slice test gives rank two, and the invertible slice prevents rank one. Explicitly put $r=\sqrt t$ and compute $P_+=(a+rb)(c+rd)$, $P_-=(a-rb)(c-rd)$. The output coefficients are $(P_++P_-)/2$ and $(P_+-P_-)/(2r)$, using two products. If $t<0$, the quotient has no real eigenvalues, so rank is greater than two; the three-product algorithm makes it exactly three.

At $t=0$, use the invertible slice $B$ as the first slice. Its quotient with $A$ is $B^{-1}A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, nonzero nilpotent. Swapping slices is a coordinate permutation and does not change tensor rank. The slice test therefore again gives rank greater than two, and the algorithm gives rank three. A repeated eigenvalue is not enough for diagonalisation; the nonzero nilpotent part is the obstruction.
\end{solution}

\begin{proposition}[Hom is left exact]\label{prop:homleft}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Exactness of $0\to A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C$ implies exactness of
\[
0\to\operatorname{Hom}(M,A)\xrightarrow{f_*}\operatorname{Hom}(M,B)
\xrightarrow{g_*}\operatorname{Hom}(M,C).
\]
\item Exactness of $A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C\to0$ implies exactness of
\[
0\to\operatorname{Hom}(C,N)\xrightarrow{g^*}\operatorname{Hom}(B,N)
\xrightarrow{f^*}\operatorname{Hom}(A,N).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
lemma:
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:testexact}
Let $A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C$ be module maps. If, for every module $N$,
\[
0\to\operatorname{Hom}(C,N)\xrightarrow{g^*}\operatorname{Hom}(B,N)
\xrightarrow{f^*}\operatorname{Hom}(A,N)
\]
is exact, then $A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C\to0$ is exact.
\end{lemma}
corollary:
\begin{corollary}[tensor is right exact]\label{cor:rightexact}
For an exact sequence $A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C\to0$ and any module $N$, the sequence
\[
A\otimes N\xrightarrow{f\otimes1}B\otimes N
\xrightarrow{g\otimes1}C\otimes N\to0
\]
is exact.
\end{corollary}
definition:
\begin{definition}\label{def:exact}
For consecutive homomorphisms
\[
\cdots\longrightarrow M_{i-1}\xrightarrow{f_{i-1}}M_i
\xrightarrow{f_i}M_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots,
\]
\emph{exactness at $M_i$} means $\operatorname{im}f_{i-1}=\ker f_i$. The sequence is \emph{exact} if this holds at each term that has both a preceding and a following map. A \emph{short exact sequence} has the form
\[
0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow f B\xrightarrow g C\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective, and $f(A)=\ker g$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:ses}
Neither
\[

\quad\text{nor}\quad
0\to\Z/2\xrightarrow{\,2\,}\Z/4\to\Z/2\to0
\]
splits. In the second sequence the first map sends $\bar a$ modulo $2$ to $\overline{2a}$ modulo $4$. A split first sequence would give $\Z\cong\Z\oplus\Z/2$, although the right side has a non-zero element of finite order and the left side does not. A split second sequence would give $\Z/4\cong\Z/2\oplus\Z/2$, although only the left side has an element of order $4$. In particular, the two end modules do not determine the middle one.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:zmzn}
For positive integers $m,n$,
\[
\Z/m\otimes_\Z\Z/n\cong(\Z/n)/m(\Z/n)
\cong\Z/\gcd(m,n).
\]
The first isomorphism uses (d), and the second uses $m\Z+n\Z=\gcd(m,n)\Z$. Thus $\Z/4\otimes\Z/6\cong\Z/2$, whereas $\Z/2\otimes\Z/3=0$.

More generally, tensoring $\Z^a\oplus\bigoplus_i\Z/m_i$ with $\Z^b\oplus\bigoplus_j\Z/n_j$ gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Z^{ab}\oplus\bigoplus_i(\Z/m_i)^b
\oplus\bigoplus_j(\Z/n_j)^a\\
\oplus\bigoplus_{i,j}\Z/\gcd(m_i,n_j).
\end{gathered}
\]
Parts (a)--(c), together with the PID structure theorem of Volume~3, Theorem~7.6, therefore compute every tensor product of finitely generated abelian groups.

For vector spaces with bases $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, the same direct-sum calculation gives the basis $(e_i\otimes f_j)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$ of $V\otimes_KW$. In particular $\dim(V\otimes W)=\dim V\dim W$, including zero and infinite cardinal dimensions.
\end{example}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:tensoralgebra}
For commutative $R$-algebras $A,B$, use the multiplication $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$ on $A\otimes_RB$; you may assume that it makes this a commutative ring. Prove the ring isomorphisms

\qquad

In particular, explain why the second tensor product is a field. Derive and use $R[X]/(p)\otimes_RA\cong A[X]/(p)$.

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch03-quotients}
Let $I,J$ be ideals of $R$. Construct a natural isomorphism
\[
(R/I)\otimes_R(R/J)\cong R/(I+J)
\]
by specifying it on pure tensors and writing its inverse. Compute $(\Z/12)\otimes_\Z(\Z/18)$. Then take $R=K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ and compute $(R/(\varepsilon))\otimes_R(R/(\varepsilon))$. Explain why the last tensor product does not recover the non-zero nilpotent element of $R$.

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch03-snake}
Let $m,n\ge1$, put $d=\gcd(m,n)$, and form a diagram with both rows $0\to\Z\xrightarrow{m}\Z\to\Z/m\to0$ and all three vertical maps multiplication by $n$. Compute the snake map
\[
\partial\colon\ker(n\colon\Z/m\to\Z/m)\longrightarrow\Z/n.
\]
Show that it sends the class of $m/d$ to the class of $n/d$, that it is injective, and that its image is the kernel of multiplication by $m$ on $\Z/n$. Work out $m=6,n=4$ explicitly.
\end{exercise}

For arbitrary vector spaces $V,W$ over $K$, prove that
\[
V^*\otimes_KW\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,W),
\qquad \varphi\otimes w\longmapsto(v\mapsto\varphi(v)w)
\]
is injective and has image exactly the maps of finite rank. For $V=W=\bigoplus_{j\ge1}Ke_j$, show that the identity is not in the image. Explain why the map is surjective whenever either $V$ or $W$ is finite-dimensional, including the zero-dimensional cases.
\end{exercise}

\begin{solution}{ex:zmzncomp}
\idea A map out of a cyclic group is determined by one element. In a tensor, divisibility lets us move an annihilating integer onto the torsion factor.
\writeup Put $d=\gcd(m,n)$. A homomorphism $\Z/m\to\Z/n$ is determined by $x=u(\bar1)$ with $mx=0$. The solutions are precisely
\[
x=\overline{j(n/d)},\qquad j=0,\ldots,d-1.
\]
Indeed, writing $m=dm_0,n=dn_0$ with $(m_0,n_0)=1$, the congruence $n\mid mx$ is equivalent to $n_0\mid x$. Addition of homomorphisms adds these images, so evaluation at $\bar1$ identifies the Hom-group with the cyclic subgroup generated by $\overline{n/d}$, of order $d$.

For $d_0\in D$ and $t\in T$, choose $n\ge1$ with $nt=0$, and choose $d_1\in D$ with $nd_1=d_0$. Then
\[
d_0\otimes t=nd_1\otimes t=d_1\otimes nt=0.
\]
Every element is a sum of pure tensors, so the whole tensor product is zero. The group $\Q$ is divisible and $\Q/\Z$ is torsion, giving the requested instance.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:composite}
\idea Quotient maps provide the arrows on the right. Exactness amounts to lifting a representative and subtracting something from the preceding image.
\writeup Write the sequence as
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\to\ker f\xrightarrow{\iota}\ker(gf)\xrightarrow f\ker g
\xrightarrow{q}B/f(A)\\
\xrightarrow{\bar g}C/gf(A)\xrightarrow{p}C/g(B)\to0,
\end{gathered}
\]
where $q(b)=b+f(A)$, $\bar g(b+f(A))=g(b)+gf(A)$, and $p$ is the natural quotient. Changing $b$ by $f(a)$ changes $g(b)$ by $gf(a)$, so $\bar g$ is well defined. The other maps are restrictions or quotient maps and are linear.

The map $\iota$ is injective. An $a\in\ker(gf)$ maps to zero under $f$ exactly when $a\in\ker f$. An element $b\in\ker g$ is killed by $q$ exactly when $b=f(a)$; then $gf(a)=0$, so $a\in\ker(gf)$.

If $\bar g([b])=0$, write $g(b)=gf(a)$. Then $b-f(a)\in\ker g$ and $q(b-f(a))=[b]$. Conversely, $g$ kills every element of $\ker g$, so $\bar gq=0$. This proves exactness at $B/f(A)$.

A class $[c]\in C/gf(A)$ lies in $\ker p$ precisely when $c\in g(B)$, which says that it is in $\operatorname{im}\bar g$. Finally $p$ is onto because every class modulo $g(B)$ has a representative in $C$. These checks prove exactness everywhere.

In the snake-lemma derivation from the hint, the connecting map is $\bar g\colon\operatorname{coker}f\to\operatorname{coker}(gf)$. The map $\ker g\to\operatorname{coker}f$ precedes it and is induced by the quotient of $B$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:qnotproj}
\idea Coordinates of a free abelian group take integer values. A divisible source cannot have a non-zero image in any such coordinate.
\writeup (a) If $u\colon\Q\to\Z$, then for $q\in\Q$ and every $n\ge1$,
\[
u(q)=n\,u(q/n).
\]
An integer divisible by every $n$ is zero: for a non-zero integer $a$, choose $n>|a|$. Thus $u=0$. If $\Q$ were projective, it would embed as a summand in some free abelian group $\bigoplus_{s\in S}\Z$. A non-zero image vector has a non-zero coordinate; composing the embedding with that coordinate projection would give a non-zero map $\Q\to\Z$, a contradiction. Since free modules are projective, this also proves that $\Q$ is not free.

(b) For finitely many injective modules $E_1,\ldots,E_r$, extend each component of a map $A\to\bigoplus_iE_i$ across $A\subseteq B$. The finitely many extensions combine to a map into that direct sum. The empty sum is zero and is injective as well.

For the decomposition of $\Q/\Z$, each summand $\Z[1/p]/\Z$ embeds through its rational representatives. Given a fraction $a/n$, factor $n=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{k_i}$. The integers $n/p_i^{k_i}$ have greatest common divisor $1$, so choose $c_i$ with
\[
\sum_i c_i\frac{n}{p_i^{k_i}}=1.
\]
Then $a/n=\sum_i ac_i/p_i^{k_i}$ is a finite sum of classes from the indicated summands. Thus the sum map is onto.

For uniqueness, suppose $\sum_{i=1}^r x_i=0$ where the order of $x_i$ is a power of the distinct prime $p_i$. For a fixed $i$, multiplying by a product of sufficiently large powers of the other primes kills all $x_j$, $j\ne i$. That product is relatively prime to the order of $x_i$, so multiplication by it is invertible on the cyclic group generated by $x_i$, and $x_i=0$. The sum map is injective. Each summand is divisible: multiplication by a prime different from $p$ is invertible on each finite $p$-power subgroup, and division by $p$ is obtained by increasing a denominator. Hence each is injective by Corollary~\ref{cor:divisible}.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:tensoralgebra}
\idea A polynomial presentation turns tensoring into a change of coefficient ring. Factorisation of the defining polynomial then decides whether the result splits or remains a field.
\writeup As an $R$-module, $R[X]=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}RX^j$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:tensorrules} gives $R[X]\otimes_RA\cong A[X]$. Tensor the right-exact presentation
\[
R[X]\xrightarrow{\,p\,}R[X]\to R[X]/(p)\to0.
\]
The induced map on $A[X]$ is multiplication by $p$, now with coefficients mapped to $A$. Its cokernel is $A[X]/(p)$. The resulting isomorphism sends $(f+(p))\otimes a$ to $af+(p)$; checking products of pure tensors shows that it is a ring isomorphism.

Apply this to $\C=\R[X]/(X^2+1)$. Over $\C$, the factors $X-i$ and $X+i$ generate comaximal ideals because their difference is the non-zero constant $2i$. The Chinese remainder theorem, Volume~3, Theorem~6.9, gives
\[
\C\otimes_\R\C\cong\C[X]/(X^2+1)\cong\C\times\C.
\]

For the second example, use $\Q(\sqrt3)=\Q[X]/(X^2-3)$ and change coefficients to $\Q(\sqrt2)$. If $a+b\sqrt2$, with rational $a,b$, squared to $3$, comparison of coefficients would give
\[
a^2+2b^2=3,\qquad 2ab=0.
\]
If $b=0$, a rational square would be $3$, impossible by its odd $3$-adic exponent. If $a=0$, a rational square would be $3/2$, again impossible by its prime exponents. Thus $X^2-3$ has no root over $\Q(\sqrt2)$ and, being quadratic, is irreducible there. Its quotient is the field $\Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:fivelemma}
\idea Prove injectivity and surjectivity separately. Exactness moves a vanishing image one position left; the hypotheses on the vertical maps let us move between rows.
\writeup Denote the horizontal arrows by $\alpha_i\colon A_i\to A_{i+1}$ and $\beta_i\colon B_i\to B_{i+1}$. The squares say $h_{i+1}\alpha_i=\beta_i h_i$.

For injectivity, let $h_3(x)=0$. Then $h_4(\alpha_3x)=\beta_3h_3x=0$, and injectivity of $h_4$ gives $\alpha_3x=0$. Write $x=\alpha_2w$. Now $\beta_2h_2w=h_3x=0$, so $h_2w=\beta_1v'$ for some $v'\in B_1$. Choose $v\in A_1$ with $h_1v=v'$. Commutativity gives
\[
h_2(\alpha_1v)=\beta_1h_1v=\beta_1v'=h_2w.
\]
Since $h_2$ is injective, $w=\alpha_1v$, and $x=\alpha_2\alpha_1v=0$.

For surjectivity, take $y\in B_3$. Choose $z\in A_4$ with $h_4z=\beta_3y$. Then
\[
h_5(\alpha_4z)=\beta_4h_4z=\beta_4\beta_3y=0.
\]
Injectivity of $h_5$ gives $\alpha_4z=0$, so $z=\alpha_3x$ for some $x\in A_3$. Hence $\beta_3(y-h_3x)=0$. Write $y-h_3x=\beta_2u'$ with $u'\in B_2$, and lift $u'=h_2u$. Finally
\[
y=h_3x+\beta_2h_2u=h_3(x+\alpha_2u).
\]
Thus $h_3$ is onto and injective.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch03-quotients}
\idea Both ideals must act by zero on the tensor product. Their sum is exactly the relation needed on the resulting cyclic module.
\writeup The rule $\bar a\otimes\bar b\mapsto ab+(I+J)$ is bilinear and independent of representatives: changing $a$ by an element of $I$, or $b$ by an element of $J$, changes the product by an element of $I+J$. It therefore defines a linear map $u$ to $R/(I+J)$.

Define $v(r+(I+J))=\bar1\otimes\bar r$. If $i\in I$, then $\bar1\otimes\bar i=\bar i\otimes\bar1=0$ because $i$ is zero in the first factor. A $j\in J$ is already zero in the second factor. Thus $v$ is well defined and linear. The composite $uv$ fixes $\bar r$. Conversely,
\[
vu(\bar a\otimes\bar b)=\bar1\otimes\overline{ab}
=\bar a\otimes\bar b.
\]
The maps are inverse, and their formulas commute with all maps induced by ring maps respecting the ideals.

For integers $(12)+(18)=(6)$, so the tensor product is $\Z/6$. For the ring with $\varepsilon^2=0$ and $I=J=(\varepsilon)$, the answer is $R/(\varepsilon)\cong K$. The tensor factors already make $\varepsilon$ act as zero; taking their tensor product cannot restore its non-zero class in $R$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch03-snake}
\idea Follow an integer representative through the snake construction, then express the kernel as a cyclic subgroup.
\writeup For $\bar k\in\ker n$ on $\Z/m$, the integer $nk$ is divisible by $m$. Lift $\bar k$ to $k\in\Z$, map it down to $nk$, and pull it back through multiplication by $m$. This gives
\[
\partial(\bar k)=\overline{nk/m}\quad\hbox{in }\Z/n.
\]
Changing $k$ to $k+mt$ changes this value by $nt$, so the formula is well defined. Write $m=dm_0,n=dn_0$ with $(m_0,n_0)=1$. The condition $m\mid nk$ is equivalent to $m_0\mid k$. Thus the kernel is generated by the class of $m_0=m/d$, of order $d$. Its image is the class of $n_0=n/d$, also of order $d$, so $\partial$ is injective. The elements killed by $m$ in $\Z/n$ are exactly the multiples of $n_0$, proving the image assertion.

For $m=6,n=4$, the kernel in $\Z/6$ is $\{\bar0,\bar3\}$, and the image in $\Z/4$ is $\{\bar0,\bar2\}$. The map sends $\bar3$ to $\bar2$. If $d=1$, both groups are zero; the same formula still applies.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch03-idempotent}
\idea An idempotent separates a module into the part on which it acts as identity and the part on which it acts as zero.
\writeup Every $r$ equals $er+(1-e)r$. If $x\in eR\cap(1-e)R$, then $ex=x$ from the first membership, while $ex=e(1-e)r=0$ from the second. Thus the sum is direct. The summand $eR$ of the free module $R$ is projective and flat by Proposition~\ref{prop:projective}.

Multiplication gives $u\colon eR\otimes_RM\to eM$, $er\otimes m\mapsto erm$. Define $v\colon eM\to eR\otimes_RM$ by $v(x)=e\otimes x$ for $x\in eM$. This is a well-defined linear map on the submodule $eM$ itself. Its composite with $u$ sends $x$ to $ex=x$. On a pure tensor,
\[
vu(er\otimes m)=e\otimes erm=er\otimes em=er\otimes m,
\]
since $er\otimes em=e(er)\otimes m=er\otimes m$. Hence $u,v$ are inverse.

Modulo $6$, $e=3$ satisfies $e^2=e$, and $eR=\{0,3\}\cong\Z/2$ as an abelian group. The other summand is $4R=\{0,2,4\}\cong\Z/3$. Proposition~\ref{prop:projective}(c) assumes a domain; $\Z/6$ has non-zero zero divisors. Also projectivity here is over $\Z/6$, not over $\Z$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch03-finiterank}
\idea A finite tensor expression has a finite-dimensional output space. Conversely, choose coordinates on the finite-dimensional image of a linear map.
\writeup Write a tensor as $t=\sum_{i=1}^r\varphi_i\otimes w_i$. Its associated map has image in the span of the finitely many $w_i$, so has finite rank. Choose a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ of that span and rewrite $t=\sum_{j=1}^s\psi_j\otimes u_j$. If its map is zero, then for every $v\in V$,
\[
\sum_j\psi_j(v)u_j=0.
\]
Independence of the $u_j$ gives $\psi_j(v)=0$ for every $j,v$. Hence all $\psi_j$ vanish and $t=0$. This proves injectivity without any dimension restriction on $V$.

If $T\colon V\to W$ has finite-dimensional image with basis $u_1,\ldots,u_s$, let $\lambda_j$ be its coordinate functionals and put $\psi_j=\lambda_jT\in V^*$. Then $T(v)=\sum_j\psi_j(v)u_j$, so $T$ is the image of $\sum_j\psi_j\otimes u_j$. This proves the image assertion.

The identity on $\bigoplus_{j\ge1}Ke_j$ has infinite-dimensional image, so it cannot come from the tensor product. If either the domain or codomain is finite-dimensional, every linear map has finite rank and the map is onto. If either space is zero, both the tensor product and the Hom-space are zero, so it is still an isomorphism.
\end{solution}

Suppose $p=\sum_{j=1}^s c_jX^{\beta_j}g_{i_j}$, where $c_j\in K$ and all the polynomials $X^{\beta_j}g_{i_j}$ have the same leading monomial $X^\delta$. If $p=0$ or $\operatorname{LM}(p)<X^\delta$, then $p$ is a $K$-linear combination of polynomials

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:colouring}
Let a finite graph $\Gamma$ have vertices $1,\ldots,n$, and set $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Prove that a proper three-colouring exists exactly when the polynomials
\[
X_v^3-1\quad(v\text{ a vertex}),\qquad
X_u^2+X_uX_v+X_v^2\quad(uv\text{ an edge})
\]
have a common zero in $\C^n$. Prove that this is equivalent to their not generating the unit ideal.
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch04-finitefield}
Let $K$ have $q$ elements and let $n\ge0$. Prove
\[
I(K^n)=(X_1^q-X_1,\ldots,X_n^q-X_n).
\]
Show that every function $K^n\to K$ is represented by a unique polynomial having degree less than $q$ in each variable. Deduce that this ideal is radical and that every subset of $K^n$ is Zariski closed. Explain the convention when $n=0$.
\end{exercise}

\begin{solution}{ex:radicals}
\idea Factor the equations to find the pieces, then check primality of their ideals to establish irreducibility.
\writeup The factorisation $X^2-Y^2=(X-Y)(X+Y)$ gives the two lines $Y=X$ and $Y=-X$. Their ideals are $(X-Y)$ and $(X+Y)$, with quotient $\C[X]$, a domain. Thus both are irreducible, and neither contains the other.

The equations $XY=XZ=YZ=0$ allow at most one non-zero coordinate. Their zero set is the union of the three coordinate axes, whose ideals are $(X,Y),(X,Z),(Y,Z)$. Each quotient is a polynomial ring in one variable, so these are three distinct irreducible components.

The equations $X^2Y=XY^2=0$ have exactly the zeros of $XY=0$: if neither coordinate is zero, neither equation can hold. Any polynomial vanishing on both axes is divisible by both $X$ and $Y$, hence by $XY$, using the UFD property. Therefore its vanishing ideal is $(XY)$. In agreement with the Nullstellensatz,
\[
\sqrt{(X^2Y,XY^2)}=(XY),
\]
since $(XY)^2=X\cdot XY^2$ lies in the given ideal, while that ideal is contained in the radical ideal $(XY)$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:colouring}
\idea Use distinct cube roots as colours, and an edge equation that vanishes exactly for two different roots.
\writeup The equations $X_v^3-1=0$ assign each vertex one of $1,\omega,\omega^2$. For two such values $x,y$, the factorisation
\[
(x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2)=x^3-y^3=0
\]
shows that the edge polynomial vanishes when $x\ne y$. If $x=y$, it equals $3x^2$, which is non-zero in $\C$. Thus its vanishing is exactly the requirement of different colours at the edge ends. Assignments solving all equations are precisely proper three-colourings.

The weak Nullstellensatz says that the equations have a common zero exactly when their ideal is proper. If the graph has no vertices, the polynomial ring is $\C$, the ideal is zero, and the unique empty assignment is the empty colouring, so the conclusion still holds.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:groebnerhand}
\idea Cancel leading terms until the new leading monomials account for every S-polynomial. Then use the surviving monomials to check the quotient as well as its points.
\writeup Put $g_1=X^2-Y$ and $g_2=X^3-X$. Their first S-polynomial is
\[
g_2-Xg_1=XY-X=:g_3.
\]
Its leading monomial $XY$ is divisible by neither $X^2$ nor $X^3$, so add it. Next,
\[
Yg_1-Xg_3=X^2-Y^2
\]
reduces by $g_1$ to $Y-Y^2$. Add its negative $g_4=Y^2-Y$. Since $g_2=Xg_1+g_3$, it is redundant. For the remaining list $g_1,g_3,g_4$, the three pairs give
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(g_1,g_3)&=X^2-Y^2\ \longrightarrow\ Y-Y^2=-g_4,\\
S(g_3,g_4)&=Yg_3-Xg_4=0,\\
S(g_1,g_4)&=Y^2g_1-X^2g_4=X^2Y-Y^3.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last polynomial reduces by $Yg_1$ to $Y^2-Y^3=-Yg_4$, hence to zero. Buchberger's criterion proves that
\[
G=\{X^2-Y,XY-X,Y^2-Y\}
\]
is a Gröbner basis.

The equation $Y^2=Y$ gives $Y=0$ or $1$. When $Y=0$, $XY-X=0$ gives $X=0$. When $Y=1$, $X^2=1$ gives $X=\pm1$. Thus $V(I)=\{(0,0),(1,1),(-1,1)\}$.

The monomials not divisible by $X^2,XY,Y^2$ are $1,X,Y$, so division shows that their classes span the quotient. They are independent: a non-zero linear combination cannot belong to $I$, because its leading monomial is divisible by none of the leading generators. Evaluation on the three points gives a map from this three-dimensional quotient to $\C^3$. On $a+bX+cY$ its values are
\[
(a,\ a+b+c,\ a-b+c).
\]
These determine $a$, then $b$ by the difference of the last two values, and $c$ by their sum. Hence evaluation is an isomorphism. The ring $\C^3$ has no non-zero nilpotents, so the quotient has none, which means $I$ is radical.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch04-finitefield}
\idea Reduce exponents one variable at a time, then use the root bound to prove uniqueness. Interpolation gives every possible function.
\writeup Every $a\in K$ satisfies $a^q=a$, by the finite-field multiplicative-group result of Volume~3, Chapter~9 (and trivially for $a=0$). Thus $J=(X_i^q-X_i)_i$ is contained in $I(K^n)$. Division by each monic $X_i^q-X_i$ reduces an arbitrary polynomial modulo $J$ to one with degree less than $q$ in each variable.

Such a reduced polynomial vanishing on $K^n$ must be zero. For $n=1$, this is the degree bound on roots. Inductively write it as a polynomial in $X_n$ with reduced coefficients in the first $n-1$ variables. At each choice of the first $n-1$ coordinates, the resulting polynomial in $X_n$ has degree less than $q$ and vanishes at all $q$ elements, so all its coefficients vanish at that choice. Induction makes every coefficient polynomial zero. Therefore $I(K^n)=J$, and reduced representatives of a function are unique.

For existence, let
\[
\ell_a(T)=\prod_{b\in K\setminus\{a\}}\frac{T-b}{a-b},
\qquad a\in K.
\]
Each denominator is non-zero. This polynomial has value $1$ at $a$ and $0$ elsewhere. For $f\colon K^n\to K$, the polynomial
\[
\sum_{a\in K^n} f(a)\prod_{i=1}^n\ell_{a_i}(X_i)
\]
has the required values and degrees. Evaluation consequently identifies $K[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/J$ with the product of one copy of $K$ for each point. A product of fields has no non-zero nilpotents, so $J$ is radical. For any subset $S$, interpolate a function equal to $0$ on $S$ and $1$ off $S$; its zero set is exactly $S$.

When $n=0$, $K^0$ consists of one empty tuple, the polynomial ring is $K$, and the ideal generated by the empty list is zero. A function on the one point is represented by its constant value, so all conclusions hold with empty products equal to $1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch04-squarezero}
\idea The ideal kills all monomials of total degree at least two, while its radical kills the two linear coordinates as well.
\writeup Since $X^2,Y^2\in J$, we have $X,Y\in\sqrt J$. Also $J\subseteq(X,Y)$ and the quotient by $(X,Y)$ is the field $K$, so this maximal ideal is radical. Therefore $\sqrt J=(X,Y)$. The zero set is the single point $(0,0)$ over every field.

Every monomial of degree at least two is divisible by $X^2,XY$, or $Y^2$, so the quotient is spanned by $1,\bar X,\bar Y$. No non-zero linear combination of these lies in $J$, since every monomial of every element of $J$ has degree at least two. Thus this list is a basis. The ideal $\mathfrak n=K\bar X+K\bar Y$ has square zero. For $u\in\mathfrak n$ and $a\ne0$,
\[
(a+u)^{-1}=a^{-1}-a^{-2}u,
\]
as multiplication verifies using $u^2=0$. If $a=0$, the element is square-zero and cannot be a unit in this non-zero ring: a square-zero unit would imply $1=0$. The quotient by $\sqrt J$ is just $K$, so taking the radical discards the two-dimensional square-zero ideal.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch04-twocolours}
\idea The vertex equations allow only two values, and the edge equations force a sign change. An odd number of sign changes cannot return to the starting sign.
\writeup Because the characteristic is not $2$, the roots of $T^2-1$ are the distinct elements $1,-1$. The edge equation $x_u+x_v=0$ forces opposite choices. Thus common zeros are precisely proper two-colourings encoded by these two values. The weak Nullstellensatz identifies existence of a common zero with propriety of $J$.

For an odd cycle with consecutive vertices $0,1,\ldots,2r$ and edge polynomials $e_i=X_i+X_{i+1}$ (indices modulo $2r+1$), take
\[
e_0-e_1+e_2-\cdots-e_{2r-1}+e_{2r}=2X_0.
\]
Every other variable cancels. Hence $X_0\in J$ after division by $2$. Combining with the vertex polynomial gives the explicit identity
\[
1=X_0\left(\frac12\sum_{i=0}^{2r}(-1)^ie_i\right)-(X_0^2-1)\in J.
\]
In characteristic $2$, the values $1$ and $-1$ coincide. Assigning $X_v=1$ at every vertex makes both $X_v^2-1$ and every $X_u+X_v$ vanish, even on a triangle. Its ideal is therefore proper although a triangle has no proper two-colouring. The characteristic assumption is indispensable for this encoding.
\end{solution}

\begin{lemma}[Noether's change of variables]\label{lem:noethervar}
Let $K$ be a field, $n\ge1$, and $f\in K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ nonconstant. For a sufficiently large integer $r$, substituting $x_i=y_i+x_n^{r^i}$ for $i<n$ gives
\[
 f=cx_n^N+\text{lower powers of }x_n,
\]
with $c\in K\setminus\{0\}$ and the remaining coefficients in $K[y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}]$.

\begin{definition}\label{def:localisation}
Let $S\subseteq R$ be multiplicative. The \emph{localisation} $S^{-1}R$ consists of equivalence classes of pairs $(r,s)\in R\times S$, where
\[
(r,s)\sim(r',s')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 t(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }t\in S.
\]
Write the class as $r/s$, and put
\[
\frac rs+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rs'+r's}{ss'},\qquad
\frac rs\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'}.
\]
The canonical homomorphism is $\iota(r)=r/1$. We write $R_f$ when $S=\{f^n:n\ge0\}$, and $R_{\mathfrak p}$ when $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$. For an $R$-module $M$, define $S^{-1}M$ by the same relation on pairs $(m,s)$, with the corresponding addition and scalar multiplication.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:spec}
The \emph{spectrum} $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is the set of prime ideals of $R$. Its \emph{Zariski topology} has closed sets
\[
 V(I)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\},
\]
where $I$ ranges over ideals. A ring homomorphism $\varphi\colon R\to T$ induces the continuous map $\operatorname{Spec}T\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ given by $\mathfrak q\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{solution}{ex:subringsq}
\idea Admitting a reduced fraction forces its denominator to be invertible. At a fixed prime, only the exponent of that prime matters.
\writeup Put $S=\{b\in\Z_{>0}:1/b\in R\}$. It contains $1$ and is multiplicative. If $a/b\in R$ is reduced with $b>0$, choose $u,v\in\Z$ with $ua+vb=1$. Since the subring is unital, it contains $\Z$, and
\[
 1/b=u(a/b)+v\in R.
\]
Thus every element of $R$ belongs to $S^{-1}\Z$. Conversely, every allowed fraction belongs to $R$ by the definition of $S$.

In $\Z_{(p)}$, a nonzero element has a unique expression $p^ku$ with $k\ge0$ and $u$ a unit. If an ideal is nonzero, choose an element with the smallest possible $k$. Dividing its unit factor shows that $p^k$ is in the ideal, while every other element is a multiple of $p^k$. The ideals are therefore $0$ and $p^k\Z_{(p)}$ for $k\ge0$, including the unit ideal at $k=0$. Among proper ideals, the primes are $0$ and $p\Z_{(p)}$. The latter is the closed point; the former has closure the whole two-point spectrum.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:quasicompact}
\idea A basic open cover is a claim that certain elements generate the unit ideal, and a formula for $1$ is finite.
\writeup For an ideal $I$, an element of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is outside $V(I)$ precisely when it omits at least one $f\in I$. Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Spec}R\setminus V(I)=\bigcup_{f\in I}D(f),
\]
proving that these opens form a basis. Refine an arbitrary open cover to a cover by $D(f_\lambda)$. No prime can contain all the $f_\lambda$. The ideal they generate cannot be proper, since any proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal. Thus $1=\sum_{i=1}^kr_if_{\lambda_i}$ for a finite list. If a prime missed all of these basic opens, it would contain all the $f_{\lambda_i}$ and hence $1$. They therefore form a finite subcover. Choosing one original open containing each selected basic open gives a finite subcover of the original cover. The empty spectrum needs only the empty subcover.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:hyperbola}
\idea A monic relation makes a projection finite; the reciprocal coordinate provides an obstruction for the other projection.
\writeup Sending $y$ to $x^{-1}$ identifies $A$ with $\C[x,x^{-1}]$, so the copy of $\C[x]$ is indeed a subring. If $y$ were integral over it, an equation
$y^n+p_{n-1}(x)y^{n-1}+\cdots+p_0(x)=0$ would yield
\[
1+p_{n-1}(x)x+\cdots+p_0(x)x^n=0.
\]
The left side is a polynomial with constant term $1$, and cannot vanish in the Laurent polynomial ring. Thus $A$ is not integral over $\C[x]$.

Put $s=x+y$. The relation $xy=1$ gives $y^2-sy+1=0$, so $y$ is integral over $\C[s]$. As $x=s-y$, the ring $A=\C[s,y]$ is integral over $\C[s]$ as well. The element $s$ is transcendental: any nonzero polynomial in $x+x^{-1}$ has a nonzero highest Laurent power of $x$. Hence this is a polynomial subring.

The projection to $x$ has one point above each nonzero complex number and none above $0$. For the projection to $s$, solve $x^2-sx+1=0$ and put $y=1/x$. The roots are always nonzero. There are two distinct points unless $s=2$ or $s=-2$, when there is one repeated root. Every fibre is finite and every complex value of $s$ occurs.
\end{solution}

In a local ring, the units are exactly the elements outside $\mathfrak m$. To see the nontrivial direction, a nonunit generates a proper ideal; Zorn's lemma puts that ideal in a maximal ideal, which must be $\mathfrak m$. We use the form of Zorn's lemma proved in Volume~7, Theorem~1.19. In a Noetherian ring, Proposition~\ref{prop:noetherian} already gives the required maximal ideal.

Gauss's theorem, Volume~3, Theorem~6.18, makes $\Z[x]$ a UFD. Therefore every ideal in (b) is prime. The quotient by $(p,f)$ is $\mathbb F_p[x]/(\bar f)$, a field, which verifies (c). The zero ideal is prime since $\Z[x]$ is a domain.

For example, $\sqrt5$ is integral over $\Z$, since it satisfies $x^2-5=0$. Volume~13 will study such elements in number fields. We need only their algebra here. A monic equation is equivalent to a finite module of powers; the converse uses the adjugate matrix.

There is an exact sequence of abelian groups
\[
1\longrightarrow R^\times\longrightarrow K^\times
 \xrightarrow{\,x\mapsto xR\,}\mathcal I(R)

definition:
\begin{definition}\label{def:fractional}
A \emph{fractional ideal} is a nonzero $R$-submodule $I\subseteq K$ with $dI\subseteq R$ for some $0\ne d\in R$. Its product with another fractional ideal $J$ is the submodule generated by all $xy$ with $x\in I$ and $y\in J$. Put
\[
 (R:I)=\{x\in K:xI\subseteq R\}.
\]
The ideal $I$ is \emph{invertible} if $IJ=R$ for some fractional ideal $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{solution}{ex:zsqrt5}
\idea An ideal equality needs both containments. Norm divisibility then obstructs a single generator.
\writeup Put $w=\sqrt{-5}$. The square of $\mathfrak p$ has generators $4$, $2+2w$, $-4+2w$, all in $2R$. Their combinations give $6=(2+2w)-(-4+2w)$ and $2=6-4$, so $\mathfrak p^2=2R$.

The product $\mathfrak q\bar{\mathfrak q}$ has generators $9$, $3(1-w)$, $3(1+w)$ and $6$. They belong to $3R$, and $9-6=3$ belongs to their span. Thus $\mathfrak q\bar{\mathfrak q}=3R$.

The generators of $\mathfrak p\mathfrak q$ are $6$, $2(1+w)$, $3(1+w)$ and $(1+w)^2$. Each is a multiple of $1+w$, including $6=(1+w)(1-w)$. Their difference $3(1+w)-2(1+w)=1+w$ proves $\mathfrak p\mathfrak q=(1+w)R$. Conjugation preserves $\mathfrak p$, since $1-w=2-(1+w)$, and gives $\mathfrak p\bar{\mathfrak q}=(1-w)R$.

If $\mathfrak p=gR$, the element $g\in R$ divides $2$ and $1+w$. Multiplicativity of $N$ makes the positive integer $N(g)$ divide both $4$ and $6$. Norm $1$ would make $g$ a unit and $\mathfrak p=R$, contrary to the quotient $R/\mathfrak p\cong\mathbb F_2$. Norm $2$ would require $a^2+5b^2=2$, which has no integer solution. No generator exists.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:powerseries}
\idea The first nonzero coefficient determines a power of $t$; everything following that power is a unit.
\writeup Let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_it^i$ with $a_0\ne0$. Define an inverse $g=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nt^n$ recursively by
\[
 b_0=a_0^{-1},\qquad b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^na_i b_{n-i}.
\]
The coefficient equations then give $fg=1$. All sums defining individual coefficients are finite, so no convergence is involved. A nonzero series has a least nonzero coefficient, say at degree $n$, and is $t^n$ times a unit. The product of two nonzero series has nonzero leading coefficient, making the ring a domain.

For any nonzero ideal, take the least order among its nonzero series. Removing the unit factor shows the ideal contains $t^n$, and every other element is a multiple of it. Thus every ideal is principal. The only nonzero prime is $(t)$, since a higher power fails the prime test. The fraction field is $k((t))$, the formal Laurent series with finitely many negative powers: each fraction is a power of $t$ times a unit, and each Laurent series has this form. Its valuation is the least exponent with nonzero coefficient. Nonzero constants have valuation zero; set $v(0)=+\infty$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:circle}
\idea The norm to $\R[x]$ has even degree, while a generator of the point ideal would need norm of degree one.
\writeup Division by the monic relation gives a unique expression $a+by$ with $a,b\in\R[x]$. Conjugation $y\mapsto-y$ makes
$N(a+by)=a^2+b^2(x^2-1)$ multiplicative. The square of $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $(x-1)^2$, $(x-1)y$ and $y^2=-(x-1)(x+1)$, so it lies in $(x-1)$. Conversely,
\[
 x-1=-\tfrac12\bigl((x-1)^2+y^2\bigr)\in\mathfrak m^2,
\]
proving equality.

If $\mathfrak m=(g)$, then $N(g)$ divides $(x-1)^2=N(x-1)$ and $x^2-1=N(y)$. It therefore divides a constant multiple of $x-1$. A nonzero constant norm would make $g$ a unit, because $\bar g/N(g)$ would be its inverse. This is impossible for a generator of the proper ideal with quotient $\R$. Thus $N(g)$ would have degree one.

For any nonzero $a+by$, the possible leading degrees of its norm are $2\deg a$ and $2\deg b+2$. If they agree, their real leading coefficients are positive squares and cannot cancel; if they differ, the larger survives. The degree is therefore even, contradicting degree one. This argument is where the real coefficient field matters.

After extending scalars to $\C$, put $u=x+iy$. Its inverse is $x-iy$, and
\[
 x=(u+u^{-1})/2,\qquad y=(u-u^{-1})/(2i).
\]
These formulas give mutually inverse ring maps with $\C[u,u^{-1}]$. It is the localisation of the PID $\C[u]$ at powers of $u$, so every ideal is the extension of its principal contraction and is principal. In particular, the extended point ideal becomes principal. The discussion does not require the quoted computation of the whole real class group.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:cubicnotprincipal}
\idea Norm degrees rule out a generator; squarefree denominators establish normality.
\writeup Put $h=x^3-x$. For (a), division by the monic polynomial $Y^2-h$ gives the unique remainder $a+bY$ over $\C[x]$. Conjugation $y\mapsto-y$ is a ring automorphism, so $N(\alpha)=\alpha\bar\alpha$ is multiplicative. If $b\ne0$, the degrees $2\deg a$ and $2\deg b+3$ have different parity; they cannot cancel. Interpreting the absent term as having degree $-\infty$, we get
\[
 \deg N(a+by)=\max(2\deg a,2\deg b+3)
\]
for a nonzero element. A unit must have constant nonzero norm, forcing $b=0$ and $a$ constant. Every such constant is indeed a unit.

For (b), $\mathfrak m^2=(x^2,xy,y^2)\subseteq(x)$. Also $x=x^3-y^2\in\mathfrak m^2$, because $x^3=x\cdot x^2$ and $y^2$ are in that ideal. Thus $\mathfrak m^2=(x)$. If $\mathfrak m=(g)$, the norm $N(g)$ divides both $x^2$ and $-h=-x(x-1)(x+1)$, so it divides $x$. It cannot be constant, for that would make $g$ a unit while $A/\mathfrak m\cong\C$. It would have degree one, excluded by the degree formula in (a).

For (c), the simple roots of $h$ ensure that it is not a square in $\C(x)$, so the fraction field is the quadratic field $\C(x)(y)$. Let $\alpha=a+by$ in that field be integral over $A$. Since $A$ is integral over $\C[x]$, transitivity makes $\alpha$ integral over $\C[x]$. Its conjugate is integral too. Thus $2a$ and $a^2-b^2h$ are integral elements of $\C(x)$, and normality of the PID $\C[x]$ puts them in $\C[x]$. Hence $a\in\C[x]$ and $b^2h\in\C[x]$. A prime factor in a reduced denominator of $b$ would occur at least twice in the denominator of $b^2$, while $h$ contains it at most once. No such factor is possible, so $b\in\C[x]$ and $\alpha\in A$.

The squarefree hypothesis is doing a specific job. For $y^2=x^3$, the fraction $y/x$ satisfies $(y/x)^2=x$ but is not in the function ring. Its denominator is possible because the cubic has a repeated root. This is an obstruction to applying the Dedekind argument to that singular curve.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch06-arithmetic}
\idea Read each operation one valuation at a time, remembering that a larger exponent means a smaller ideal.
\writeup At $\mathfrak p$, the exponents of $I,J$ are $2,1$; at $\mathfrak q$ they are $1,3$. Every other exponent is zero. Hence
\[
 I+J=\mathfrak p\mathfrak q,\quad
 I\cap J=\mathfrak p^2\mathfrak q^3,\quad
 IJ=\mathfrak p^3\mathfrak q^4.
\]
Neither ideal contains the other, since the inequalities go in opposite directions at the two primes. Multiplying $xJ\subseteq I$ by $J^{-1}$ shows $xR\subseteq IJ^{-1}$, equivalent to $x\in IJ^{-1}$. Conversely membership in $IJ^{-1}$ gives the required containment. Thus $(I:J)=IJ^{-1}=\mathfrak p\mathfrak q^{-2}$.

Over $\Z$, $I=(12)$ and $J=(54)$. Their sum is $(6)$, their intersection $(108)$, their product $(648)$ and their fractional colon $(2/9)\Z$. For example, $x\cdot54\in12\Z$ exactly when $x\in(2/9)\Z$. Finally, $\mathfrak p^2$ and $\mathfrak q$ are coprime, and their product is their intersection, so
$R/I\cong R/\mathfrak p^2\times R/\mathfrak q$ by the Chinese remainder theorem. The numerical case gives $\Z/12\cong\Z/4\times\Z/3$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch06-gaussian}
\idea Factor the reduced quadratic and keep repeated factors as multiplicities.
\writeup The Gaussian integers are a Euclidean domain, hence a PID and Dedekind; their fraction field is quadratic over $\Q$. Since $(1+i)^2=2i$ and $i$ is a unit, $2S=(1+i)^2S$. Its prime quotient is $\mathbb F_2$, so $e=2$ and $f=1$.

Modulo $3$, the polynomial $T^2+1$ has no root: the squares in $\mathbb F_3$ are $0,1$. It is irreducible, so $S/3S=\mathbb F_3[T]/(T^2+1)$ is the field with nine elements. Thus $3S$ is prime, with $e=1$ and $f=2$.

Finally, $5=(2+i)(2-i)$. The quotient by $(2+i)$ sends $i$ to $-2=3$ modulo $5$, while the quotient by $(2-i)$ sends $i$ to $2$. These are distinct prime ideals with quotients $\mathbb F_5$. Each has $e=f=1$. The three sums are respectively $2\cdot1$, $1\cdot2$ and $1\cdot1+1\cdot1$, all equal to $2$.

The quotient modulo $2$ is $\mathbb F_2[T]/((T+1)^2)$. It has a single prime, the ideal of $T+1$, but a nonzero nilpotent class $T+1$. This extra layer records multiplicity. It cannot be replaced by two distinct primes, which would instead give a product of two fields with no nonzero nilpotents.
\end{solution}

theorem:
\begin{theorem}[long exact sequences]\label{thm:les}
An exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ induces the four long exact sequences below:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\cdots\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(A,N)\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(B,N)
\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(C,N)\\
\to A\otimes N\to B\otimes N\to C\otimes N\to0,\\[2pt]
\cdots\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(M,C)
\to M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to M\otimes C\to0,\\[2pt]
0\to\operatorname{Hom}(C,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}(B,N)
\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,N)\\
\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(C,N)\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(B,N)\to\cdots,\\[2pt]
0\to\operatorname{Hom}(M,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}(M,B)
\to\operatorname{Hom}(M,C)\\
\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(M,A)\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(M,B)\to\cdots.
\end{gathered}
\]
In every degree the connecting maps lower the Tor index by one and raise the Ext index by one. The other maps follow the covariances in Proposition~\ref{prop:torextbasic}.
\end{theorem}
definition:
\begin{definition}\label{def:resolution}
A \emph{projective resolution} of an $R$-module $M$ is an exact augmented sequence
\[
\cdots\longrightarrow P_2\xrightarrow{d_2}P_1
\xrightarrow{d_1}P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}M\longrightarrow0
\]
in which every $P_n$ is projective. The notation $P_\bullet\to M$ includes the augmentation $\varepsilon$. The underlying complex $P_\bullet$ ends in $P_0\to0$; it has $H_0(P_\bullet)\cong M$ and $H_n(P_\bullet)=0$ for $n>0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:torext}
For a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to M$ and an $R$-module $N$, define
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(M,N)=H_n(P_\bullet\otimes_R N),\qquad
\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(M,N)=H^n(\operatorname{Hom}_R(P_\bullet,N)).
\]
In the tensor complex the differential is $d_n\otimes1$. In the Hom cochain complex the map from degree $n$ to degree $n+1$ sends $u:P_n\to N$ to $u\circ d_{n+1}$. Thus cohomology means kernel modulo image with the arrows pointing towards increasing degrees.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:torextz}
Let $n\ge1$ and let $N$ be an abelian group. Resolve $\Z/n$ by multiplication by $n$. Tensoring produces $N\xrightarrow{n}N$; Hom produces the same map, because a homomorphism $\Z\to N$ is determined by its value at $1$. Consequently
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/n,N)\cong N[n]=\{x\in N:nx=0\},\qquad
\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/n,N)\cong N/nN.
\]
Both constructions vanish in degrees at least two. For positive integers $m,n$, putting $d=\gcd(m,n)$ gives
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/m,\Z/n)\cong\Z/d,
\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/m,\Z/n)\cong\Z/d.
\]
In contrast, $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/n,\Z)\cong\Z/n$. The kernel $N[n]$ is the $n$-torsion in $N$: this calculation explains the name Tor.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:extzp}
For a prime $p$, the group $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/p,\Z/p)\cong\Z/p$ gives exactly $p$ equivalence classes of extensions with these ends. The zero class has middle group $(\Z/p)^2$. The other $p-1$ classes all have middle group $\Z/p^2$, with different prescribed maps: for $a=1,\ldots,p-1$, take
\[
j(n)=pn,\qquad q(x)=ax\pmod p.
\]
Exercise~\ref{ex:extzp2} computes the corresponding class as $a^{-1}$ modulo $p$. For $p=2$ this leaves just one nonsplit class. For $p=3$ two different extension classes have the same middle group $\Z/9$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:rp2uct}
For the projective plane, Figure~\ref{fig:surfaces} gives the boundary complex
$\Z\xrightarrow{2}\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z$ in degrees $2,1,0$. Its integer homology is
$H_0=\Z$, $H_1=\Z/2$, $H_2=0$. After tensoring with $\Z/2$, both differentials are zero and the top homology becomes $\Z/2$.
The first universal coefficient sequence explains where the new class came from:
\[
H_2(C\otimes\Z/2)\cong
(H_2(C)\otimes\Z/2)\oplus\operatorname{Tor}_1(H_1(C),\Z/2)
\cong0\oplus\Z/2.
\]
For integer cohomology, the second sequence instead gives
$H^2(\operatorname{Hom}(C,\Z))\cong\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/2,\Z)\cong\Z/2$.
The top integer homology is zero, while top integer cohomology is not: the torsion from degree one appears one degree higher in cohomology.
\end{example}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:baersum}
Let $0\to N\xrightarrow{j_i}E_i\xrightarrow{q_i}M\to0$ be extensions for $i=1,2$. Form
\[
X=\{(e_1,e_2):q_1(e_1)=q_2(e_2)\},\qquad
E=X/\{(j_1(n),-j_2(n)):n\in N\}.
\]
Prove that $E$ is an extension of $M$ by $N$, using the common quotient map and the induced inclusion of $N$. Show that
$\Theta(E)=\Theta(E_1)+\Theta(E_2)$ in the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:extclass}. This construction is the \emph{Baer sum}.
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch07-dualnumbers}
Let $R=K[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ and $k=R/(\epsilon)$. Check that
\[
\cdots\xrightarrow{\epsilon}R\xrightarrow{\epsilon}R
\xrightarrow{\epsilon}R\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow0
\]
is a free resolution. Compute $\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(k,k)$ and
$\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(k,k)$ for every $n\ge0$, and use the answer to prove that $k$ has no projective resolution of finite length.
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[$\star\star$]\label{ex:v10new-ch07-connecting}
Fix positive integers $r,s$. In the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow\Z/r\xrightarrow{j}\Z/(rs)
\xrightarrow{q}\Z/s\longrightarrow0,
\qquad j(a)=sa,\quad q(b)=b\pmod s,
\]
compute the connecting image of $\mathrm{id}_{\Z/s}$ in
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/s,\Z/r)\cong(\Z/r)/s(\Z/r)$, with the lift convention of Theorem~\ref{thm:extclass}. Determine exactly when the sequence splits, and give a section whenever it does.
\end{exercise}
