\begin{solution}{ex:kleinuct}
\idea Keep the single nonzero boundary matrix visible, then compare its kernel and cokernel over each coefficient group.
\writeup Over $\Z$, the map $t\mapsto(0,2t)$ is injective. Therefore
$H_2=0$, $H_1=\Z^2/\langle(0,2)\rangle\cong\Z\oplus\Z/2$, and $H_0=\Z$.
Over $\Z/2$ the whole differential is zero, giving $H_2=\Z/2$, $H_1=(\Z/2)^2$, $H_0=\Z/2$.
Over $\Q$ the nonzero boundary spans the second coordinate, so $H_2=0$, $H_1=\Q$, $H_0=\Q$.

For universal coefficients, the degree-two tensor term from $H_2$ is zero, while
$\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z\oplus\Z/2,A)\cong A[2]$.
Thus $A=\Z/2$ creates precisely the computed top class, and $A=\Z$ or $\Q$ does not. In degree one the Tor term from $H_0=\Z$ vanishes, and
$H_1\otimes A\cong A\oplus A/2A$, giving the same answers.

With integer cochains the complex is
$\Z\xrightarrow0\Z^2\xrightarrow{(0\ \ 2)}\Z$.
Hence $H^0=\Z$, $H^1=\{(u,0):u\in\Z\}\cong\Z$, and $H^2=\Z/2$. The cohomology sequence gives the degree-one term
$\operatorname{Hom}(\Z\oplus\Z/2,\Z)=\Z$, with zero Ext from $H_0$; in degree two it gives
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z\oplus\Z/2,\Z)=\Z/2$, with zero Hom from $H_2$. Groups in all other degrees vanish.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:torsym}
\idea Decompose both finitely generated groups into free and cyclic parts, for which first Tor is already known.
\writeup A finite direct sum of projective resolutions is a resolution of the direct sum. Tensor distributes over that sum, and the kernels and images of a finite direct sum are the corresponding sums of kernels and images. Consequently first Tor is additive in each variable. Write
\[
M\cong\Z^a\oplus\bigoplus_i\Z/m_i,
\qquad N\cong\Z^b\oplus\bigoplus_j\Z/n_j.
\]
Terms involving $\Z$ vanish: in the first variable it is projective, and in the second it is flat. Each remaining term is $\Z/\gcd(m_i,n_j)$ by Example~\ref{ex:torextz}. Thus both orders of the two variables give a finite direct sum of the same finite cyclic groups. This proves the claimed isomorphism and finiteness without using the general quoted symmetry theorem.
For Ext, the same example gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/2,\Z)=\Z/2$, while projectivity of $\Z$ gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z,\Z/2)=0$. They are not isomorphic.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:koszul}
\idea The two variables act as zero on $K$, while the dual Koszul complex over $R$ retains its nonzero maps.
\writeup The resolution checked at the start is
$0\to R\xrightarrow{(-y,x)}R^2\xrightarrow{(x\ \ y)}R\to K\to0$.
After tensoring with $K$, every entry $x,y$ becomes zero. Thus the complex is $0\to K\xrightarrow0K^2\xrightarrow0K\to0$, and
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_0^R(K,K)=K,\quad
\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(K,K)=K^2,\quad
\operatorname{Tor}_2^R(K,K)=K,
\]
with zero groups in larger degrees.

Applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,R)$ instead gives
\[
0\longrightarrow R\xrightarrow{c\mapsto(cx,cy)}R^2
\xrightarrow{(a,b)\mapsto-ay+bx}R\longrightarrow0.
\]
The first map has zero kernel, so $\operatorname{Ext}^0=0$. If $-ay+bx=0$, reduction modulo $x$ shows $x\mid a$, say $a=cx$; substitution gives $b=cy$. Hence the middle kernel is the first image and $\operatorname{Ext}^1=0$. The final image is $(x,y)$, so
$\operatorname{Ext}^2\cong R/(x,y)=K$. All later groups vanish. This works in every characteristic, including characteristic two: the signs change their appearance but the displayed compositions and divisibility arguments remain valid.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:extzp2}
\idea Evaluate the lifted defining relation $p$ and express the result through the specified injection.
\writeup Multiplication by $p$ injects $\Z/p$ into $\Z/p^2$ with image $p\Z/p^2$. Since $a$ is a unit modulo $p$, this image is exactly $\ker q$ and $q$ is onto. Thus we do have an extension.
Use $P=\Z$, $K=p\Z$, $\pi(1)=1$. Choose $u\in\Z/p^2$ with $au\equiv1\pmod p$ and define $\beta(1)=u$. Then
$\beta(p)=pu=j(u\bmod p)$, so the relation map has $\varphi(p)=a^{-1}\pmod p$.
Every restriction to $p\Z$ of a map $\Z\to\Z/p$ is zero, since it sends $p$ to $p$ times its value at $1$. Therefore evaluation at $p$ identifies the Ext quotient with $\Z/p$, and gives exactly the asserted class. These $p-1$ nonzero classes are distinct.

One can also check the maps directly. An equivalence $E_a\to E_b$ is multiplication by a unit $u$ modulo $p^2$. Compatibility with $j$ forces $u\equiv1\pmod p$; compatibility with the quotient maps forces $bu\equiv a\pmod p$. Hence $b=a$. Together with the split class this accounts for all $p$ extensions.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:baersum}
\idea Form pairs above the same quotient element, then identify the two kernel copies by addition.
\writeup The set $X$ is a submodule of $E_1\oplus E_2$, and
$D=\{(j_1(n),-j_2(n)):n\in N\}$ is a submodule of $X$. Define
\[
j(n)=[(j_1(n),0)]=[(0,j_2(n))],\qquad
q[(e_1,e_2)]=q_1(e_1)=q_2(e_2).
\]
The quotient map is well defined because $D$ maps to zero. It is onto: choose one preimage of a given $m$ in each $E_i$. If $j(n)=0$, there is $n'$ with
$(j_1(n),0)=(j_1(n'),-j_2(n'))$; injectivity of $j_2$ gives $n'=0$, and injectivity of $j_1$ gives $n=0$. If $q[(e_1,e_2)]=0$, write $e_i=j_i(n_i)$. Its class is $j(n_1+n_2)$, which proves exactness.

Fix the projective presentation used in Theorem~\ref{thm:extclass}, and choose lifts $\beta_i:P\to E_i$ with $\beta_i\iota=j_i\varphi_i$. The pair $(\beta_1,\beta_2)$ lands in $X$ and gives a lift $\beta$ to $E$. On $k\in K$ its class is
$[(j_1\varphi_1(k),j_2\varphi_2(k))]=j(\varphi_1(k)+\varphi_2(k))$.
It follows that $\Theta(E)=[\varphi_1+\varphi_2]$, the sum of the two Ext classes. Independence from the chosen lifts follows from the already proved independence in that theorem.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:extqz}
\idea An injective coefficient group turns Ext into a quotient of Hom, and factorial denominators give many compatible homomorphisms.
\writeup Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:les} in the second variable to
$0\to\Z\to\Q\to\Q/\Z\to0$. Since $\Q$ is divisible, it is injective by Chapter~3, and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Q,\Q)=0$. Also $\operatorname{Hom}(\Q,\Z)=0$: the image of a rational must be divisible by every positive integer, so is zero. Every homomorphism $\Q\to\Q$ is multiplication by a rational $c$, since its value at $1$ determines its values at $1/n$ and then at every rational. The long exact sequence therefore identifies
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Q,\Z)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}(\Q,\Q/\Z)/\{q\mapsto cq+\Z:c\in\Q\}.
\]
The displayed copy of $\Q$ is injected: if $cq\in\Z$ for every rational $q$, then $c=0$.

Set $x_n=u(1/n!)$ for $n\ge1$. Compatibility requires
$(n+1)x_{n+1}=x_n$. Conversely such a sequence defines
$u(a/n!)=ax_n$; passing to a common factorial denominator shows that this value is independent of the representation. Start with $x_1=0$. For every chosen $x_n$, multiplication by $n+1$ on $\Q/\Z$ is onto and has exactly $n+1$ elements in each fibre. At every step one can choose between at least two continuations. Choosing two fixed continuations at each stage embeds the set of infinite binary sequences into these homomorphisms. That set is uncountable, so the Hom group is uncountable. Its quotient by the countable subgroup $\Q$ is therefore nonzero.

Choose a nonzero class and the corresponding extension
$0\to\Z\xrightarrow{j}E\xrightarrow{q}\Q\to0$.
It does not split. In fact $E$ contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\Q$. If $D\cong\Q$ were such a subgroup, the restriction $q|_D$ would be multiplication by a rational after identifying $D$ with $\Q$. It cannot be zero, because then $D$ would lie in $j(\Z)$, which contains no nonzero divisible subgroup. A nonzero rational multiplication is an isomorphism of $\Q$, so its inverse would give a section $\Q\to D\subset E$, splitting the extension. This contradiction proves $E\not\cong\Z\oplus\Q$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch07-dualnumbers}
\idea A nilpotent element can keep the same nonzero relation module alive in every degree.
\writeup Write $r=a+b\epsilon$ uniquely with $a,b\in K$. Then $\epsilon r=a\epsilon$. Its image is $K\epsilon$, and its kernel is also $K\epsilon$. The quotient map $R\to k$ has that kernel, so every place of the augmented sequence is exact. Every term is free of rank one. This verifies the resolution without appealing to a general periodic-resolution theorem.

On $k$, multiplication by $\epsilon$ is zero. Both tensoring with $k$ and applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,k)$ therefore give a complex with one copy of $k$ in each nonnegative degree and all differentials zero. Hence
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(k,k)\cong k$ and
$\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(k,k)\cong k$ for every $n\ge0$.
If a finite projective resolution of length $d$ existed, its tensor complex would have no terms in degree $d+1$ and would give zero Tor there. Independence of resolutions contradicts the nonzero group just computed. Thus no such finite resolution exists.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch07-connecting}
\idea The connecting class records what happens to a lifted defining relation of the quotient.
\writeup The standard presentation of $\Z/s$ is
$s\Z\hookrightarrow\Z\to\Z/s$. Lift $1\in\Z$ to $1\in\Z/(rs)$. Its relation $s$ maps to $s=j(1)$, so the relation map sends $s$ to $1\in\Z/r$. The connecting class is therefore
$[1]\in(\Z/r)/s(\Z/r)$ with the stated convention. Exactness of the Hom--Ext sequence says that the identity lifts to a section precisely when this class is zero. This happens exactly when $1$ lies in $s(\Z/r)$, or equivalently $\gcd(r,s)=1$.

For a direct section in that case, choose $v$ with $rv\equiv1\pmod s$ and put $t=rv\in\Z/(rs)$. Then $q(t)=1$ and $st=srv=0$ modulo $rs$. Sending $\bar k\in\Z/s$ to $kt$ is well defined and is a section. The formulas also handle $r=1$ or $s=1$: the zero end group causes no exception. If the gcd is larger than one, the nonzero class proves nonsplitting.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch07-coefficients}
\idea Separate kernel and cokernel of the same multiplication map; dualising reverses which degree receives each one.
\writeup Tensoring gives $A\xrightarrow{m}A\xrightarrow0A$ in degrees $2,1,0$. Thus
\[
H_2=A[m],\qquad H_1=A/mA,\qquad H_0=A,
\]
and all other groups vanish. The Hom cochain complex is
$A\xrightarrow0A\xrightarrow{m}A$, giving
\[
H^0=A,\qquad H^1=A[m],\qquad H^2=A/mA,
\]
with zero groups elsewhere.

The integer homology is $H_0(C)=\Z$, $H_1(C)=\Z/m$, $H_2(C)=0$. In degree two the tensor sequence contributes
$\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/m,A)=A[m]$, despite $H_2(C)=0$. In degree one it gives $(\Z/m)\otimes A=A/mA$ and no Tor from $H_0$. For cohomology, degree one is
$\operatorname{Hom}(\Z/m,A)=A[m]$, while degree two is
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/m,A)=A/mA$. These identifications also hold when $m=1$, where both middle torsion terms vanish.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch07-splitting}
\idea A chain automorphism can fix the two outside terms of an exact sequence while shearing its middle term.
\writeup Since $d_1(x,y)=2x$, the integer kernel is
$\{(0,y):y\in\Z\}$ and the cokernel is $\Z/2$. Thus
$H_1(C)=\Z$, generated by $(0,1)$, and $H_0(C)=\Z/2$.
The map $F$ is a chain map because $d_1F_1(x,y)=2x=F_0d_1(x,y)$; its inverse replaces $y+x$ by $y-x$. On both integer homology groups it acts as the identity.

After tensoring with $\Z/2$, the differential is zero and
$H_1(C\otimes\Z/2)=(\Z/2)^2$, $H_0(C\otimes\Z/2)=\Z/2$. In degree one the universal coefficient sequence is
\[
0\longrightarrow\Z/2\xrightarrow{y\mapsto(0,y)}
(\Z/2)^2\xrightarrow{(x,y)\mapsto x}\Z/2\longrightarrow0.
\]
The last coordinate description follows either from the connecting chase or from lifting the boundary generator $2$ by $(1,0)$. The induced middle map is
$(x,y)\mapsto(x,y+x)$, while the outside maps are identity maps. A section must send $1$ to $(1,a)$ for some $a\in\Z/2$. Commuting with $F$ would require
$(1,a+1)=(1,a)$, which is impossible. Thus no splitting for this object commutes with its automorphism $F$. A splitting natural in all chain maps would have to commute with every chain automorphism, proving the claimed obstruction.
\end{solution}
cross_volume_reference_lines: Here $R$ is a commutative ring with identity, and every module is unital. We use the chain complexes and chain homotopies introduced in Volume~9, Chapter~6. Their proofs used addition and homomorphisms only, so they apply to $R$-modules. For reference, a chain complex has maps $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ with $d_nd_{n+1}=0$. Its cycles and boundaries are $Z_n=\ker d_n$ and $B_n=\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$, and its homology is $Z_n/B_n$. Unless stated otherwise, complexes vanish in negative degrees.

It splits in each degree. Tensor and Hom both preserve split exact sequences, so applying either produces a short exact sequence of complexes, with the order reversed for Hom. The zigzag lemma proved in Volume~9, Lemma~6.2, now gives the first and third long sequences. For a cochain complex the same chase raises the index instead of lowering it. Proposition~\ref{prop:torextbasic}(b) identifies the degree-zero ends. The inclusion and projection of these resolutions lift the original module maps, so their induced maps are the functorial ones just defined.

We work first with algebraic complexes of finitely generated free modules. The examples from polygons use the finite boundary complexes already computed in Volume~9, Chapter~6. This avoids assuming a comparison theorem for arbitrary cell structures or a freeness theorem for infinitely generated modules.

This is an algebraic statement about a chain complex and its dual. The general de Rham theorem, quoted in Volume~9, Chapter~3, needs a separate comparison between differential forms and singular cochains. Coefficient duality alone does not prove that comparison.

theorem:
\begin{theorem}[Hilbert, Noether, Speiser]\label{thm:hilbert90}
For a finite Galois extension $L/K$ with group $G$,
\[
H^1(G,L^\times)=1,\qquad H^1(G,L)=0.
\]
The first expression uses multiplicative notation and the second additive notation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:h2cyclic}
For a cyclic group $G$ of order $n\ge1$ acting on $A$, there is an isomorphism
\[
H^2(G,A)\cong A^G/N(A).
\]
For $a\in A^G$, the corresponding class has representative
\[
f_a(\sigma^i,\sigma^j)=
\begin{cases}a&i+j\ge n,\\0&i+j<n,\end{cases}
\qquad 0\le i,j<n.
\]
\end{theorem}
proposition:
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:complements}
Complements of $A$ in $A\rtimes G$ are exactly the graphs
\[
K_f=\{(f(g),g):g\in G\},\qquad f\in Z^1(G,A).
\]
Two such complements are conjugate by an element of $A$ exactly when their cocycles differ by an element of $B^1(G,A)$. Thus $H^1(G,A)$ parametrises the $A$-conjugacy classes of complements.
\end{proposition}
example:
\begin{example}[carrying]\label{ex:carry}
Fix an integer base $b\ge2$ and give $A=\Z/b$ the trivial action of $G=\Z/b$. Then $A^G=A$ and $N(A)=bA=0$, so
$H^2(\Z/b,\Z/b)\cong\Z/b$.
The usual carry cocycle is $f_1(x,y)=1$ if $x+y\ge b$ and zero otherwise, for standard digit representatives $0\le x,y<b$. The map
$(a,x)\mapsto ba+x\pmod{b^2}$ identifies its extension with $\Z/b^2$.

Multiplying the cocycle by $a\in\Z/b$ gives all $b$ extension classes. The zero class gives $(\Z/b)^2$. In the class with carry $a$, the lift $t=(0,1)$ satisfies $t^b=(a,0)$. Its order is $b$ times the order of $a$: a power can be the identity only when its exponent is divisible by $b$, and the remaining condition is that the corresponding multiple of $a$ vanish. The group is abelian because the action is trivial and the carry is symmetric. It is generated by the kernel and $t$, so every element is killed by $b$ times the order of $a$. Hence the middle group is cyclic of order $b^2$ exactly when $a$ is a unit modulo $b$. There are $\varphi(b)$ such extension classes. For $b=10$, the remaining nonzero classes have types $\Z/20\times\Z/5$ and $\Z/50\times\Z/2$, as computed in Exercise~\ref{ex:carry10}.
\end{example}

\begin{solution}{ex:carry10}
\idea The carry extension is an abelian group with two generators and two relations, so its element orders determine the finite abelian type.
\writeup Trivial action and symmetry of the carry make $E_a$ abelian. Its generators $u=(1,0)$ and $t=(0,1)$ satisfy
$10u=0$, $10t=au$, and its order is $100$ because its underlying set is $(\Z/10)^2$. The order of $t$ is $10$ times the order of $a$ in $\Z/10$.
If $a=1,3,7,9$, this is $100$, so $t$ generates $E_a\cong\Z/100$.
If $a=5$, it is $20$. Both generators are killed by $20$, so the exponent is exactly $20$. The classification of finite abelian groups now gives $\Z/20\times\Z/5$: its two-primary part has order four and exponent four, and its five-primary part has order $25$ and exponent five.
If $a=2,4,6,8$, the order of $t$ is $50$ and the exponent is $50$. The five-primary part is cyclic of order $25$ and the two-primary part is $(\Z/2)^2$, giving $\Z/50\times\Z/2$.
For $a=0$, the multiplication has no carry and is the direct product $(\Z/10)^2$.
The theorem gives distinct extension classes for distinct $a$. Thus exactly $\varphi(10)=4$ inequivalent extensions share the cyclic middle group $\Z/100$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:quaternion}
\idea Associativity of the quaternion multiplication produces the cocycle automatically; its diagonal values prevent it from being a coboundary.
\writeup In multiplicative notation the table of
$f(g,h)=s(g)s(h)s(gh)^{-1}$ is
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
f&1&\bar i&\bar j&\bar k\\\hline
1&1&1&1&1\\
\bar i&1&-1&1&-1\\
\bar j&1&-1&-1&1\\
\bar k&1&1&-1&-1
\end{array}
\]
For example, $ij=k$ gives $f(\bar i,\bar j)=1$, whereas $ji=-k$ gives $f(\bar j,\bar i)=-1$. The kernel is central, so the action is trivial.
If $f=db$ for $b:G\to\{\pm1\}$, normalisation gives $b(1)=f(1,1)=1$. But then
$(db)(\bar i,\bar i)=b(\bar i)^2b(1)^{-1}=1$, contradicting the table entry $-1$. Thus the class is nonzero.

A complement would have order four and meet $\{\pm1\}$ only in $1$. Every element outside $\{\pm1\}$ has square $-1$, so any subgroup containing such an element also contains $-1$. A subgroup of order four must contain one, making the intersection nontrivial. No complement exists. Theorem~\ref{thm:h2ext} therefore gives the same nonzero conclusion from nonsplitting.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:cyclich1}
\idea The value on a cyclic generator determines a crossed homomorphism, and the full cycle gives its only restriction.
\writeup If $x=f(\sigma)$, repeated use of the cocycle identity gives
$f(\sigma^i)=x+\sigma x+\cdots+\sigma^{i-1}x$.
The relation $\sigma^n=1$ forces $N(x)=0$. Conversely, for $x\in\ker N$ this formula defines a one-cocycle: concatenating partial sums proves the identity until an exponent reaches $n$, and a wraparound changes the sum by $N(x)=0$. A principal cocycle has generator value $(\sigma-1)a$. These values lie in $\ker N$ because $N(\sigma-1)=0$, giving
$H^1(G,A)\cong\ker N/(\sigma-1)A$.
For $n=1$, $N=1$, both sides are zero and the same description holds.

For a cyclic Galois extension and additive $A=L$, vanishing says precisely that every trace-zero $x$ is $\sigma(a)-a$, equivalently $b-\sigma(b)$ after replacing $a$ by $-b$. For multiplicative $A=L^\times$, the same argument uses products: generator values have norm one and principal values are $\sigma(a)/a$, equivalently $b/\sigma(b)$ after inversion. Thus each cyclic vanishing statement implies the corresponding corollary, and each assertion of the corollary kills every one-cocycle in that cyclic action. This establishes the claimed cyclic equivalence. It makes no reduction of a general finite Galois group to a cyclic one.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:artinschreier}
\idea In characteristic $p$, the constant $-1$ has trace zero, so the additive theorem supplies an element shifted by one.
\writeup The trace of $-1$ is $-p=0$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:hilbert90}, write
$-1=b-\sigma(b)$ and put $\alpha=b$. Then $\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha+1$. Induction gives
$\sigma^i(\alpha)=\alpha+i$ for $0\le i<p$. These are distinct, since the prime subfield has $p$ elements. In particular $\alpha\notin K$, and the tower law in the degree-$p$ extension forces $K(\alpha)=L$.
The characteristic-$p$ binomial formula gives
\[
\sigma(\alpha^p-\alpha)
=(\alpha+1)^p-(\alpha+1)=\alpha^p-\alpha.
\]
This element is fixed by the generating automorphism, hence by all of $G$, so it is $a\in K$. Thus $\alpha$ is a root of $x^p-x-a$, and its degree is $p$. The argument includes $p=2$; there $-1=1$ and the same equations remain valid.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:order20}
\idea The normal Sylow subgroup supplies an abelian kernel of coprime index. Classifying its complement actions then gives a short list of groups.
\writeup The number of Sylow five-subgroups divides four and is congruent to one modulo five, so it is one. Its unique subgroup $A$ is cyclic of order five and normal. Theorem~\ref{thm:sz} gives a complement $Q$ of order four, so
$E\cong A\rtimes_\rho Q$, where
$\rho:Q\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)\cong\Z/4$.
Changing generators of $Q$ precomposes $\rho$ with an automorphism; changing a generator of $A$ conjugates the image in its automorphism group, which is abelian and thus leaves that image action unchanged.

If $Q=\Z/4$, the image of a generator can have order one, two or four. The two order-four choices are exchanged by the automorphism that inverts the generator. The three resulting groups are the cyclic group $\Z/20$, the inversion-action semidirect product (the dicyclic group of order $20$), and the faithful-action group of affine maps $x\mapsto ax+b$ of $\mathbb F_5$.
If $Q=(\Z/2)^2$, the image is trivial or has order two. All three nonzero maps to the order-two subgroup of $\Z/4$ differ by automorphisms of $Q$. The resulting groups are
$\Z/5\times(\Z/2)^2\cong\Z/10\times\Z/2$ and the dihedral group of order $20$.

This list exhausts all homomorphisms and hence all groups. To separate its entries, their Sylow two-subgroups distinguish the cyclic-complement cases from the elementary-abelian-complement cases. In each family the trivial action gives an abelian group and the nontrivial action does not. Of the two remaining nonabelian cyclic-complement groups, the inversion-action group has centre of order two, generated by the square of its complement generator; the faithful affine group has trivial centre. Indeed a central element must centralise $A$, forcing its complement component to lie in the action kernel, and it must be fixed by the complement, forcing its $A$ component to be zero in either nontrivial action. The five groups are therefore pairwise nonisomorphic.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch08-inversion}
\idea Inversion makes every possible generator value a one-cocycle, while only the two fixed elements can be powers of an extension lift.
\writeup The invariant subgroup of $\Z/4$ is $\{0,2\}\cong\Z/2$, so $H^0\cong\Z/2$. A one-cocycle is determined by $x=f(\sigma)$, and the relation requires $x+\sigma x=x-x=0$, which always holds. Principal values are $-2a$, whose subgroup is $\{0,2\}$. Therefore $H^1\cong(\Z/4)/\{0,2\}\cong\Z/2$. The norm $1+\sigma$ is zero, giving $H^2\cong\{0,2\}\cong\Z/2$.

Write the generator of the kernel multiplicatively as $u$, of order four, and a lift of $\sigma$ as $t$. The action gives $tut^{-1}=u^{-1}$. The two possible classes are represented by $t^2=1$ and $t^2=u^2$. Both groups have order eight by their cocycle construction, and every element is $u^i$ or $u^it$ for $0\le i<4$.
For $t^2=1$, all four elements $u^it$ are involutions, and $u^2$ is another one. This is the usual rotation-reflection presentation of the dihedral group of the square.
For $t^2=u^2$, one has $(u^it)^2=t^2=u^2$ for every $i$, so all four outside elements have order four; among the kernel elements only $u^2$ is an involution. Sending $u\mapsto i$, $t\mapsto j$ identifies this presentation with $Q_8$, since $jij^{-1}=i^{-1}$ and $j^2=i^2=-1$. The different involution counts distinguish the middle groups as well as the extension classes.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch08-affine}
\idea The relation $I+T+T^2=0$ removes the one-cocycle constraint, but an integer index-three image leaves a nonzero quotient.
\writeup Direct multiplication gives $T^2+T+I=0$ and $T^3=I$. The fixed equations
$(-b,a-b)=(a,b)$ imply $a=-b$ and $a=2b$, hence $3b=0$ in $\Z$ and $a=b=0$. Thus $H^0=0$. A one-cocycle is determined by $x=f(\sigma)$, and the sole cyclic condition is
$(I+T+T^2)x=0$, which holds for every $x\in\Z^2$. Conversely the partial sums $0,x,x+Tx$ define a one-cocycle because their full sum is zero. Principal values are $(T-I)A$.

For $(a,b)\in\Z^2$,
$(T-I)(a,b)=(-a-b,a-2b)$.
Its two coordinates sum to $-3b$, so this image lies in
$\{(r,s):r+s\equiv0\pmod3\}$. Conversely, if $r+s$ is divisible by three, put $b=-(r+s)/3$ and $a=-r-b$; these integers give the required preimage. Hence

The affine map $F(v)=Tv+x$ with $x=(1,0)$ satisfies
$F^3(v)=T^3v+(I+T+T^2)x=v$, and it is not the identity since $F(0)=x\ne0$. Thus its order is three. Solving $(I-T)v=x$ gives $v=(2/3,1/3)$, so there is a rational fixed point. \idea The norm-one identity makes $1+x$ a useful eigenvector for conjugation; only its possible vanishing needs a separate choice.
\writeup If $x=1$, take $b=1$ in every characteristic. If $x\ne1$ and $x\ne-1$, take $b=1+x$. It is nonzero and
$\sigma(b)=1+x^{-1}=x^{-1}(1+x)$, so $b/\sigma(b)=x$.
The same formula also works for any $x\ne-1$ without the initial separation of $x=1$ whenever $1+x\ne0$.
If $x=-1\ne1$, the characteristic is not two. Choose $c\in L\setminus K$ and let $b=c-\sigma(c)$. It is nonzero, since the fixed field of $\sigma$ is $K$, and $\sigma(b)=-b$, giving $b/\sigma(b)=-1$. \begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch08-averaging}
\idea Inverting the group order on the coefficient group turns the averaged coboundary formulas into primitives of the original cocycles.
\writeup Let $u:A\to A$ be the inverse of multiplication by $m$. It is an additive automorphism. It commutes with each $G$-action map: both $g\cdot u(a)$ and $u(g\cdot a)$ are the unique element whose $m$-fold multiple is $g\cdot a$. Applying $u$ pointwise to cochains therefore commutes with the coboundary $d$.

For a one-cocycle, put $b=\sum_gf(g)$. The calculation of Proposition~\ref{prop:killed} gives $mf=d(-b)$. Apply $u$ to obtain
$f=d(-u(b))$. For a two-cocycle put $c(g)=\sum_kf(g,k)$; the same proposition gives $mf=dc$, hence $f=d(u\circ c)$. Every cocycle in these two degrees is a coboundary, proving both vanishing statements.
If $A$ is a vector space over a field where $m\ne0$, scalar multiplication by $m$ has inverse scalar multiplication by $m^{-1}$. The hypotheses therefore hold for characteristic zero and for characteristic prime to $m$, in any dimension and over any such field. Only sums indexed by the finite group were used, so the size of the coefficient group need not be finite.
\end{solution}

\begin{theorem}[Wedderburn, 1908]\label{thm:wedderburn}
Suppose that the left regular module of $A$ is a finite direct sum of simple modules. Then there are division rings $D_i$ and positive integers $n_i$ such that
\[
A\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i).
\]
If $A$ is a finite-dimensional complex algebra, each $D_i$ is $\C$. For the zero ring, the product is empty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Frobenius reciprocity, 1898]\label{thm:frobrecip}
For a $G$-representation $V$ and an $H$-representation $W$, evaluation at $1$ gives an isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(\operatorname{Res}_HV,W),
\qquad T\longmapsto(v\longmapsto T(v)(1)).
\]
Thus induction is right adjoint to restriction. For characters, with the inner product convention of Volume~3,
\[
\langle\chi_V,\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\psi\rangle_G
=\langle\operatorname{Res}_H\chi_V,\psi\rangle_H.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mackey, 1951]\label{thm:mackey}
Choose one representative $s$ of each double coset in $H\backslash G/K$. Then
\[
\operatorname{Res}_K\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW
\cong\bigoplus_s\operatorname{Ind}_{K_s}^KW^{(s)}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:endA}
For a unital ring $A$, right multiplication gives an isomorphism of rings
\[
A^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_A(A),\qquad
 a\longmapsto R_a,\quad R_a(x)=xa.
\]
Here $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same elements and addition as $A$, with multiplication reversed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:wedderburnCG}
Let $V_1,\ldots,V_r$ represent the irreducible complex representations of $G$, with characters $\chi_i$ and dimensions $d_i$. The action maps give an algebra isomorphism
\[
\C[G]\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^r\operatorname{End}(V_i)
\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{d_i}(\C),\qquad
 a\longmapsto(\rho_i(a))_i.
\]
The centre is spanned by the conjugacy-class sums and becomes the product of the scalar matrices. Its element
\[
e_i=\frac{d_i}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi_i(g^{-1})g
\]
acts as the identity on $V_i$ and as zero on every $V_j$ with $j\ne i$. In particular the $e_i$ are the central idempotents selecting the individual blocks.
\end{corollary}
definition:
\begin{definition}\label{def:induced}
The representation of $G$ induced from $W$ is
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW
=\{f:G\to W:\ f(hx)=h\cdot f(x)
\text{ for }h\in H, x\in G\}.
\]
Its action is $(g\cdot f)(x)=f(xg)$. Restriction, written $\operatorname{Res}_HV$, keeps the vector space of a $G$-representation $V$ and uses only the action of $H$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:dihedral}
Write $D_n=\langle r,s:r^n=s^2=1, srs^{-1}=r^{-1}\rangle$, of order $2n$, with $n\ge2$. Its rotation subgroup $H=\langle r\rangle$ has index $2$. Put $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$ and $\psi_j(r^k)=\zeta^{jk}$.

No reflection is conjugate into $H$, so its induced character is zero. The two cosets of $H$ give, on a rotation,
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_H^{D_n}\psi_j(r^k)
=\zeta^{jk}+\zeta^{-jk}=2\cos(2\pi jk/n).
\]
For $0<j<n/2$, this is the character of a two-dimensional irreducible representation. It can be realised by a plane rotation through $2\pi j/n$ and a reflection. Exercise~\ref{ex:dihedralmackey} checks irreducibility and fills in the one-dimensional cases.
\end{example}

\begin{solution}{ex:doublecosets}
\idea A trivial representation contributes one invariant vector in every Mackey summand.
\writeup Reciprocity and Mackey give
\[
\langle\operatorname{Ind}_H1,\operatorname{Ind}_K1\rangle_G
=\sum_{HsK}\langle\operatorname{Ind}_{K_s}^K1,1\rangle_K
=\sum_{HsK}1.
\]
For the last equality use reciprocity once more: the restriction of a trivial representation is trivial.

Take $K=H$. Orbits of the diagonal action on $G/H\times G/H$ correspond to $H$-orbits on the second coordinate after the first is moved to $H$. These are the double cosets $HsH$. Since the action is transitive, the invariant functions on $X$ are exactly the constant functions: the trivial representation occurs once. Write the rest as $\bigoplus_i m_iV_i$ with nontrivial irreducibles. Then the permutation character has squared norm $1+\sum_i m_i^2$. This is $2$ precisely when the remainder is one irreducible occurring once. For $|X|\ge2$, the diagonal and the distinct ordered pairs are both nonempty, so two orbits are exactly double transitivity.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:dihedralmackey}
\idea There is only one double coset outside the normal rotation subgroup.
\writeup The double cosets are $H$ and $HsH$. Conjugation by $s$ replaces $r$ by $r^{-1}$, so $\psi_j^{(s)}=\psi_{-j}$. Mackey's criterion now gives irreducibility precisely when $2j\not\equiv0\pmod n$. The characters for $j$ and $-j$ induce to the same representation, by their values in Example~\ref{ex:dihedral}.

The distinct two-dimensional representations are therefore indexed by $1\le j<n/2$. For a linear character, $r$ must equal its inverse because $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$; hence its value is $1$, or also $-1$ if $n$ is even. The value on $s$ can independently be $1$ or $-1$. There are two linear characters for odd $n$ and four for even $n$. The square sums are
\[
2+4\frac{n-1}{2}=2n\quad(n\text{ odd}),
\qquad
4+4\frac{n-2}{2}=2n\quad(n\text{ even}).
\]
They exhaust the regular representation, so no irreducible is missing. For $n=2$, the two-dimensional list is empty and the four lines describe the Klein four group.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:rq8}
\idea Separate the part where the central group element $z$ acts as $1$ from the part where it acts as $-1$.
\writeup Set $e=(1+z)/2$ and $e'=(1-z)/2$ in $\R[Q_8]$. They are central, satisfy $e+e'=1$, $ee'=0$, and are idempotent. Thus the algebra is the product of the ideals $e\R[Q_8]$ and $e'\R[Q_8]$. Each has dimension $4$: choose one representative from each pair $\{g,zg\}$ to obtain a basis $eg$, respectively $e'g$.

In the first ideal, $z$ acts as $1$, so it is the group algebra of $Q_8/\langle z\rangle\cong(\Z/2)^2$. Its four real linear characters give $\R^4$. In the second, the map induced by $Q_8\subset\mathbb H^\times$ sends $e'$ to $1$ and has image containing $1,i,j,k$. It is surjective onto $\mathbb H$ and has the same real dimension $4$, so it is an isomorphism.

After extension of scalars to $\C$, send $i,j$ to
\[
I=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix},
\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
They satisfy $I^2=J^2=-1$ and $IJ=-JI$. The four matrices $1,I,J,IJ$ are linearly independent and span $M_2(\C)$. Hence $\mathbb H\otimes_\R\C\cong M_2(\C)$, giving the claimed complex algebra and its degree sum $4\cdot1^2+2^2=8$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:heisenberg}
\idea Use the centre to distinguish the induced representations, then use the degree sum to prove completeness.
\writeup With the coordinates in the hint, multiplication is
\[
(a,b,c)(a',b',c')=(a+a',b+b',c+c'+ab').
\]
The centre is $Z=\{(0,0,c)\}$, and commutators range over all of $Z$. Therefore the linear characters are exactly the $p^2$ characters of $G/Z\cong\mathbb F_p^2$.

The subgroup $A=\{(0,b,c)\}$ is abelian, normal and of index $p$. Fix $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/p}$. For each $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p^\times$, let
$\psi_\lambda(0,b,c)=\zeta^{\lambda c}$.
Conjugation by $(a,0,0)$ changes this to $\zeta^{\lambda(c+ab)}$. For $a\ne0$, choosing $b=1$ shows that the character changes. Mackey's criterion therefore makes $\operatorname{Ind}_A^G\psi_\lambda$ irreducible of dimension $p$.

On a central element $(0,0,c)$ this representation acts as the scalar $\zeta^{\lambda c}$: the scalar is already prescribed on every induced coordinate, since the element is central. Distinct $\lambda$ give nonisomorphic representations. Their degree squares add to
\[
p^2+(p-1)p^2=p^3=|G|.
\]
Thus they, together with the linear characters, are the full list. The number is $p^2+p-1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:affinefrob}
\idea A slope gives a quotient character; the translations supply the remaining representation.
\writeup The slope homomorphism $G\to\mathbb F_q^\times$ has kernel $N$, the translations. For any nontrivial character $\psi$ of the cyclic group $H=\mathbb F_q^\times$, the character $\theta_\psi$ has degree $1$, equals $\psi(a)$ on the map $x\mapsto ax$, and equals $1$ on $N$. It is exactly $\psi$ pulled back through the slope map. These, with the trivial character, give $q-1$ linear characters.

There are $q$ conjugacy classes: the identity; one class of all nonzero translations, because scaling multiplies their parameters transitively; and one class for every slope $a\ne1$, because a translation moves its unique fixed point to any prescribed point. Thus exactly one irreducible character remains. Its degree $d$ obeys
$(q-1)+d^2=q(q-1)$, so $d=q-1$.

For a nontrivial additive character $\lambda$ of $\mathbb F_q$, conjugation by a slope $a\ne1$ changes it. Indeed invariance would give $\lambda((a-1)b)=1$ for every $b$; multiplication by $a-1$ is a bijection, forcing $\lambda$ to be trivial. Mackey's criterion proves that $\operatorname{Ind}_N^G\lambda$ is irreducible of degree $q-1$, so it is the remaining one. If $q=2$, the complement is trivial, and the same argument gives the second linear character of $G\cong\Z/2$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:centrefaithful}
\idea Scalars detect the centre; taking tensor powers makes a possible denominator grow too quickly.
\writeup Schur's lemma sends every $z\in Z(G)$ to a scalar $\lambda(z)$. For a faithful representation this embeds $Z(G)$ into $\C^\times$. A finite subgroup of order $m$ in $\C^\times$ lies among the $m$th roots of unity, by Lagrange's theorem; that set is cyclic, and so is each subgroup. Thus the centre is cyclic.

We first prove locally the degree-divisibility fact needed for the second part. Character orthogonality and Lemma~\ref{lem:omega} give
\[
\frac{|G|}{d}
=\sum_C\frac{|C|\chi(c)}{d}\,\overline{\chi(c)},
\qquad c\in C.
\]
The right side is an algebraic integer, while the left side is rational. Hence $d\mid|G|$. This also appears in Volume~3, Exercise~11.8, but the computation here makes the dependence explicit.

Now put $Z=Z(G)$ and choose any integer $m\ge1$. The representation of $G^m$ on $V^{\otimes m}$ has character $\prod_i\chi(g_i)$ and squared norm $\prod_i\langle\chi,\chi\rangle=1$, so it is irreducible of degree $d^m$. Its central subgroup
\[
Z_0=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in Z^m:z_1\cdots z_m=1\}
\]
acts trivially, since the product of its scalar actions is $\lambda(z_1\cdots z_m)=1$. The subgroup has order $|Z|^{m-1}$, so the representation descends irreducibly to a group of order $|G|^m/|Z|^{m-1}$. Degree divisibility for this quotient gives
\[
|Z|\left(\frac{[G:Z]}d\right)^m\in\Z
\qquad(m\ge1).
\]
Write $[G:Z]/d=a/b$ in lowest terms with $b>0$. The displayed integrality says $b^m\mid|Z|$ for every $m$, because $a^m$ and $b^m$ are coprime. This forces $b=1$. Thus $d$ divides $[G:Z]$, whether or not $V$ is faithful.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch09-s3idempotents}
\idea The two linear characters select the symmetric and alternating averages; the third block is what remains.
\writeup In the notation of the hint,
\[
e_+=\frac{A+B}{6},\qquad e_-=\frac{A-B}{6},
\qquad e_0=1-\frac A3=\frac{2-r-r^2}{3}.
\]
The character formula in Corollary~\ref{cor:wedderburnCG} gives exactly these expressions: the standard character has values $2,-1,0$ on the identity, three-cycles and transpositions. The relations $A^2=3A$, $AB=BA=3B$, $B^2=3A$ show $e_+^2=e_+$, $e_-^2=e_-$ and $e_+e_-=0$. They also give $(A/3)^2=A/3$, so $e_0$ is idempotent and annihilates $e_\pm$. Their sum is $1$. The ideal dimensions are $1,1,4$, either from the matrix blocks or from the independent translates of these elements. They sum to $6$, as they must.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch09-normalinduction}
\idea All double-coset intersections are the same subgroup, so only conjugation of the inducing character matters.
\writeup Since $H$ is normal, $H_s=H$. Linear characters are irreducible, and two such characters have a common constituent exactly when they agree. Mackey's criterion says that no $s\notin H$ may fix $\psi$, which is exactly the stabiliser condition.

For the affine group over $\mathbb F_7$, choose $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/7}$ and $\psi(b)=\zeta^b$ on translations. A nonidentity slope changes $\psi$ by multiplying its argument by that slope, so the stabiliser is $H$. The induced representation is irreducible of degree $6$. At the identity its character is $6$. At a translation by $b\ne0$, the six cosets yield
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_7^\times}\zeta^{ab}=-1,
\]
because the full geometric sum over $\mathbb F_7$ is zero. At an element with slope different from $1$, no conjugate belongs to the translation subgroup, so the induced character is zero. As a check, its squared norm is $(36+6)/42=1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch09-c3real}
\idea A real polynomial has one real root and one conjugate pair in this factorisation.
\writeup Let $u$ generate $\Z/3$. Every algebra element has the form $a+bu+cu^2$, so the algebra is $\R[X]/(X^3-1)$. The relatively prime factors $X-1$ and $X^2+X+1$ give the isomorphism
\[
f(u)\longmapsto(f(1),f(\zeta))\in\R\times\C.
\]
The second factor is $\C$ as a real algebra, since $\zeta$ is nonreal and satisfies the quadratic. The idempotents are $(1+u+u^2)/3$ and $1-(1+u+u^2)/3$, with ideals of real dimensions $1$ and $2$. After extension to $\C$, the quadratic splits into $(X-\zeta)(X-\bar\zeta)$, so the second ideal becomes $\C\times\C$. These are the two characters $u\mapsto\zeta$ and $u\mapsto\bar\zeta$. They combine into one simple real representation but remain distinct over $\C$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch09-primeclass}
\idea The double transpositions exhibit the normal subgroup; the action on four points gives the non-linear character.
\writeup The classes have sizes $1,3,4,4$: the identity, the three double transpositions, and the two classes of three-cycles. For a double transposition, its centraliser in $A_4$ is the Klein four group, giving class size $12/4=3$. For a three-cycle, its centraliser has order $3$, giving size $4$; the eight three-cycles therefore split into two classes. Proposition~\ref{prop:primepowerclass} proves nonsimplicity. Explicitly, the identity and the three double transpositions form the normal Klein four subgroup $V_4$; closure follows by multiplying any two distinct double transpositions.

The quotient $A_4/V_4\cong\Z/3$ gives three linear characters. Write $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and choose the two three-cycle classes to map to the two nonidentity quotient elements. Their rows are
\[
(1,1,1,1),\quad(1,1,\zeta,\zeta^2),
\quad(1,1,\zeta^2,\zeta).
\]
The four-point permutation character is $(4,0,1,1)$, so removing constants gives $(3,-1,0,0)$. Its squared norm is $(9+3)/12=1$, hence it is irreducible. The degree squares $1+1+1+9=12$ show completeness. For the three linear rows, multiplying values by class sizes yields algebraic integers immediately. For the degree-three row the scalars are $1,-1,0,0$. Thus the divisibility in Lemma~\ref{lem:omega} can be checked in every class here.
\end{solution}

\[
S^\lambda\subseteq U,
\qquad U\subseteq(S^\lambda)^\perp.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Robinson--Schensted correspondence]\label{thm:rs}
For $\sigma\in\mathfrak S_n$, insert $\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)$ successively to obtain $P(\sigma)$. In the new cell added at step $k$, place $k$ in a recording tableau $Q(\sigma)$. Then
\[
\sigma\longmapsto(P(\sigma),Q(\sigma))
\]
is a bijection between permutations and pairs of standard tableaux of the same shape. In particular,
\[
\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,
\qquad \dim S^\lambda=f^\lambda.
\]
The standard polytabloids are therefore a basis of $S^\lambda$.
\end{theorem}
definition:
\begin{definition}\label{def:partition}
A partition $\lambda\vdash n$ is a finite sequence
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k>0$ with sum $n$.
Its Young diagram consists of the cells $(i,j)$ with $1\le i\le k$ and $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, drawn with row $i$ counted from the top and column $j$ from the left. The conjugate partition has parts
\[
\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\},
\]
the column lengths. A tableau of shape $\lambda$ fills these cells with $1,\ldots,n$, each once.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:tabloid}
Two tableaux of shape $\lambda$ are row equivalent if their rows agree as sets. Their equivalence class $\{T\}$ is a tabloid. Let $M^\lambda$ be the complex vector space with the tabloids as a basis and action $\sigma\{T\}=\{\sigma T\}$.

Define the column antisymmetrizer and its polytabloid by
\[
\kappa_T=\sum_{\pi\in C_T}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\pi,
\qquad e_T=\kappa_T\{T\}.
\]
The Specht module $S^\lambda$ is the span in $M^\lambda$ of all the $e_T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:dominance}
For partitions $\lambda,\mu$ of $n$, write $\lambda\trianglerighteq\mu$ when
\[
\sum_{j=1}^i\lambda_j\ge\sum_{j=1}^i\mu_j
\quad\text{for every }i\ge1,
\]
with parts beyond the last nonzero part set equal to zero. We say that $\lambda$ dominates $\mu$.
\end{definition}

\begin{solution}{ex:catalan}
\idea The hook product counts the tableaux; row membership turns each filling into a bracket string.
\writeup In row $1$, the hooks are $n+1,n,\ldots,2$, with product $(n+1)!$. In row $2$ they are $n,n-1,\ldots,1$, with product $n!$. Therefore
\[
f^{(n,n)}=\frac{(2n)!}{(n+1)!n!}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}n.
\]
Read the labels in increasing order. Write an opening bracket when a label is in row $1$ and a closing bracket when it is in row $2$. In every initial segment, each bottom-row entry already read has a smaller top-row entry above it, so there are at least as many opening brackets as closing brackets. The total numbers agree, giving a correctly matched string.

Conversely, put the positions of the opening brackets into the top row in increasing order and the remaining positions into the bottom row. The initial-segment condition ensures that the $j$th opening bracket comes before the $j$th closing bracket, so every column increases. The two constructions are inverse. For $n=0$, the empty string and empty tableau give the same value $1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:youngmult}
\idea The column antisymmetrizer forces every map to preserve one generating line.
\writeup Given $\theta:S^\mu\to M^\mu$, extend it by zero on $(S^\mu)^\perp$ to a module map $\Theta:M^\mu\to M^\mu$. For any tableau $T$, Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}(b) gives
\[
\theta(e_T)=\kappa_T\Theta(\{T\})=c e_T.
\]
Fixing one $T$ determines the scalar $c$. For every $\sigma$,
$\theta(e_{\sigma T})=\sigma\theta(e_T)=c e_{\sigma T}$.
These polytabloids span $S^\mu$, so $\theta$ is $c$ times the inclusion. The space of such maps has dimension $1$, exactly the multiplicity of $S^\mu$ in the semisimple module $M^\mu$ by Schur's lemma. Every other constituent dominates $\mu$ by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:specht}; since its shape differs, the dominance is strict.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:frobeniusdim}
\idea Split the integers $1,\ldots,l_i$ into hooks and omitted differences.
\writeup In row $i$, hook lengths strictly decrease as the column increases. The largest is $h_{i1}=\lambda_i+k-i=l_i$, and every hook is positive. There are $\lambda_i$ distinct hooks in $\{1,\ldots,l_i\}$. The $k-i$ numbers $l_i-l_j$ for $j>i$ are also distinct and lie in that set.

They do not overlap the hooks. For $c\le\lambda_i$,
\[
h_{ic}-(l_i-l_j)=\lambda_j+\lambda'_c+1-c-j.
\]
If $\lambda_j\ge c$, then column $c$ reaches row $j$, so $\lambda'_c\ge j$ and the difference is at least $1$. If $\lambda_j<c$, then $\lambda'_c\le j-1$ and the difference is at most $-1$. It is never zero.

There are $\lambda_i+k-i=l_i$ numbers in these two disjoint lists. They therefore partition $\{1,\ldots,l_i\}$, and
\[
\prod_{c=1}^{\lambda_i}h_{ic}
=\frac{l_i!}{\prod_{j>i}(l_i-l_j)}.
\]
Multiply over $i$ and substitute into the hook length formula to obtain the stated result.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch10-standardcharacter}
\idea Remove the constant direction from the permutation representation and compute on coordinate differences.
\writeup The trace on $\C^n$ is the number $F(\sigma)$ of fixed points, since its matrix permutes the coordinate basis. The constant line contributes trace $1$. Hence
$\chi^{(n-1,1)}(\sigma)=F(\sigma)-1$.
For $a,b<n$,
\[
\langle v_a,v_b\rangle=\delta_{ab}+1,
\]
so the Gram matrix is $I_{n-1}+J_{n-1}$, where $J$ has every entry $1$. It is positive definite, since for coefficients $c_a$ the squared norm is $\sum|c_a|^2+|\sum c_a|^2$.

Let $t=(1\,n)$. Then $tv_1=-v_1$, while $tv_a=v_a-v_1$ for $2\le a<n$. Its diagonal entries in this basis are $-1,1,\ldots,1$, giving trace $n-3$. The permutation fixes $n-2$ points, so $F(t)-1=n-3$ agrees. For $n=2$ the basis consists just of $v_1$ and the trace is $-1$, as required.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch10-hookwalk}
\idea First condition on the starting cell; only afterward multiply by its uniform probability.
\writeup Name the cells of $(3,1)$ by $A=(1,1)$, $B=(1,2)$, $C=(1,3)$ and $D=(2,1)$. The corners are $C,D$. Starting from $C$ or $D$ stops there immediately. Starting from $B$ moves to $C$ with probability $1$. From $A$, the three destinations $B,C,D$ each have probability $1/3$, giving stopping probabilities $2/3$ at $C$ and $1/3$ at $D$.

Averaging the four starts gives
\[
\Pr(C)=\frac14\left(\frac23+1+1+0\right)=\frac23,
\qquad
\Pr(D)=\frac14\left(\frac13+0+0+1\right)=\frac13.
\]
These equal $f^{(2,1)}/f^{(3,1)}=2/3$ and $f^{(3)}/f^{(3,1)}=1/3$.

For $(2,2)$, the only corner is $(2,2)$. The other cells have at least one allowable move, every move increases row or column, and the diagram is finite. Thus every start reaches that corner with probability $1$. From $(1,1)$ the first move goes to $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$, each with probability $1/2$, and then the corner is forced. Multiple paths are disjoint ways of reaching the same endpoint, so their probabilities add.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch10-plancherel4}
\idea Shape probabilities count pairs of tableaux, and the first row gives the subsequence length.
\writeup In the partition order $(4),(3,1),(2,2),(2,1,1),(1^4)$, the Plancherel weights are $1,9,4,9,1$ divided by $24$. Their first-row lengths are $4,3,2,2,1$. Therefore
\[
\Pr(L=1)=\frac1{24},\quad
\Pr(L=2)=\frac{13}{24},\quad
\Pr(L=3)=\frac9{24},\quad
\Pr(L=4)=\frac1{24}.
\]
The expectation is $(1+26+27+4)/24=29/12$. The only self-conjugate shape is $(2,2)$, so its probability is $4/24=1/6$. In any self-conjugate shape, transposition pairs each cell of content $c$ with one of content $-c$. The sum of contents is zero, and Theorem~\ref{thm:transposition} gives zero character on transpositions. The converse need not follow from this cancellation argument alone.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch10-collisions}
\idea Different blocks can carry the same scalar; multiplicities belong to the whole eigenspace.
\writeup Hooks and contents give the table
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
shape&degree&content sum\\\hline
$(6)$&$1$&$15$\\
$(5,1)$&$5$&$9$\\
$(4,2)$&$9$&$5$\\
$(4,1,1)$&$10$&$3$\\
$(3,3)$&$5$&$3$\\
$(3,2,1)$&$16$&$0$\\
$(3,1,1,1)$&$10$&$-3$\\
$(2,2,2)$&$5$&$-3$\\
$(2,2,1,1)$&$9$&$-5$\\
$(2,1,1,1,1)$&$5$&$-9$\\
$(1^6)$&$1$&$-15$
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For example, $(4,1,1)$ has hooks $6,3,2,1,2,1$, whose product is $72$, and degree $720/72=10$. Its contents are $0,1,2,3,-1,-2$, summing to $3$. For $(3,3)$, the hook product is $4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=144$, giving degree $5$ and content sum $3$.

Since $\binom62=15$, exactly these two shapes give eigenvalue $1/5$. Their matrix blocks have dimensions $10^2$ and $5^2$, giving total multiplicity $125$. Giving either $100$ or $25$ alone would omit another invariant part of the same eigenspace. Conjugation negates contents and preserves degrees, so the two conjugate shapes give eigenvalue $-1/5$ with multiplicity $125$ too. The squared degrees in the table sum to $720$, checking the block dimensions against the regular representation.
\end{solution}

The diagrams now give every dimension. We need one more character value for the random-transposition walk of Volume~11. Instead of computing the whole character table, we can add a signed number over the cells. The content of $(i,j)$ is $j-i$: zero on the diagonal, positive above it and negative below it.

The same diagrams will label representations of $U(n)$, provided they have at most $n$ rows. In the next chapter, sums of eigenvalue monomials replace finite-group characters, and Haar integration replaces a finite average. The numbers $f^\lambda$ will return in moments of a random unitary trace. Volume~11 will use our transposition ratios to study how a random walk approaches its uniform law.

For every partition of $4$, calculate $f^\lambda$ and $\chi^\lambda(\tau)$ using hooks and contents. Match the results with Volume~3, Example~11.13. Then find the seven irreducible dimensions for $\mathfrak S_5$ and verify that their squares sum to $120$.

For example, $(3,1)$ has hooks $4,2,1,1$, giving degree $24/8=3$. The transposition character is $3\cdot2/6=1$. The rows match, respectively, the trivial character, the standard character $\chi_3$, the two-dimensional character obtained from $\mathfrak S_3$, the sign twist of $\chi_3$, and the sign character in Volume~3, Example~11.13.

\begin{theorem}[Peter--Weyl, 1927]\label{thm:peterweyl}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The representative functions $\mathcal R(G)$ are uniformly dense in $C(G)$.
\item The functions $\sqrt{d_\rho}\rho_{ij}$, for $\rho\in\widehat G$ and $1\le i,j\le d_\rho$, form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(G,\mu)$. With
\[
\widehat f(\rho)=\int_G f(g)\rho(g)^*\,\dd\mu(g),
\]
every $f\in L^2(G,\mu)$ has the expansion
\[
f=\sum_{\rho\in\widehat G}d_\rho\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\widehat f(\rho)\rho\bigr),
\qquad
\int_G|f|^2\,\dd\mu
=\sum_\rho d_\rho\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\widehat f(\rho)\widehat f(\rho)^*\bigr).
\]
The series for $f$ converges in $L^2$.
\item The irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis of the closed subspace of class functions. Here a class function in $L^2$ means an equivalence class satisfying $f(hgh^{-1})=f(g)$ for every fixed $h$ and almost every $g$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Diaconis--Shahshahani 1994, Rains 1998]\label{thm:traces}
For each integer $a\ge0$,
\[
(\operatorname{tr}U)^a
=\sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash a\\\ell(\lambda)\le n}}
 f^\lambda\chi_{V_\lambda}(U),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E|\operatorname{tr}U|^{2a}
=\#\{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_a:
 \text{the longest increasing subsequence of $\sigma$ has length at most $n$}\}.
\]
In particular, this moment is $a!$ whenever $a\le n$.
\end{theorem}
proposition:
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:powertraces}
For positive integers $j,k$,
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{tr}U^j]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E\bigl[\operatorname{tr}U^j\overline{\operatorname{tr}U^k}\bigr]
=\delta_{jk}\min(k,n).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{solution}{ex:dims}
\idea Cancel factors equal to $1$, then telescope the remaining products. The largest weight identifies the conjugation representation.
\writeup For $\lambda=(k,0,\ldots,0)$ only pairs $(1,l)$ contribute. Their product is
\[
\prod_{l=2}^n\frac{k+l-1}{l-1}=\binom{n+k-1}{k}.
\]
This includes $k=0$, giving the trivial representation. For $\lambda=(1^k,0^{n-k})$, the nontrivial factors have $j\le k<l$. For fixed $j$ their product is $(n-j+1)/(k-j+1)$. Multiplying over $j$ gives $\binom nk$. Empty products handle $k=0$ and $k=n$.

For $\lambda=(1,0,\ldots,0,-1)$, $n\ge2$, the pairs $(1,l)$ with $l<n$ contribute $n-1$ together, as do the pairs $(j,n)$ with $j>1$. The pair $(1,n)$ contributes $(n+1)/(n-1)$. The product is $n^2-1$. For $n=2$ the two earlier products are empty and equal $1$, giving $3$ as required.

Conjugation on $\operatorname{End}(\C^n)$ has character
$|\sum_jt_j|^2=n+\sum_{j\ne k}t_jt_k^{-1}$.
The scalar line splits off, and the trace-zero complement has character
$n-1+\sum_{j\ne k}t_jt_k^{-1}$, whose leading monomial is $t_1t_n^{-1}$. Decompose this complement into irreducibles. Its leading monomial must be the largest leading monomial of a constituent, since weight multiplicities are nonnegative. Hence $V_{(1,0,\ldots,0,-1)}$ occurs. Its dimension already equals the complement's dimension, so it is the entire complement. The action is on $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\C)$, the trace-zero matrices.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:charpoly}
\idea An alternating sum of distinct orthonormal characters has squared norm equal to the number of terms.
\writeup Diagonalization gives
$\det(I-U)=\prod_j(1-t_j)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^ke_k(t)$.
The function $e_k$ is the character of $\Lambda^k\C^n$, identified above as the irreducible of weight $(1^k,0^{n-k})$. These $n+1$ weights are distinct, including the two one-dimensional representations at $k=0,n$. Character orthogonality now kills every cross term and leaves
$\mathbb E|\det(I-U)|^2=\sum_{k=0}^n1=n+1$.
As a check, at $n=1$, $\mathbb E|1-z|^2=2$. The $k=1$ case of the quoted Keating--Snaith product also telescopes:
$\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\Gamma(j+1)\Gamma(j+3)/\Gamma(j+2)^2
=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(j+2)/(j+1)=n+1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:su2}
\idea The Vandermonde quotient becomes a sine quotient, and its apparent singularities cancel. Fourier completeness rules out missing irreducibles.
\writeup The two-variable formula gives
\[
s_{(m,0)}(e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha})
=\frac{e^{i(m+1)\alpha}-e^{-i(m+1)\alpha}}
 {e^{i\alpha}-e^{-i\alpha}}
=\frac{\sin((m+1)\alpha)}{\sin\alpha}.
\]
At $\alpha=0$ the limit is $m+1$; at $\pi$ it is $(-1)^m(m+1)$. These also follow from the scalar matrices $I$ and $-I$ acting on the symmetric power.

Using the stated density, the inner product of $\chi_m$ and $\chi_l$ is
\[
\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin((m+1)\alpha)\sin((l+1)\alpha)\,\dd\alpha
=\delta_{ml}.
\]
Complete reducibility says that a character's squared norm is the sum of the squared multiplicities of its irreducible constituents. Norm $1$ therefore makes each restriction irreducible. Their orthogonality makes them pairwise different.

If an irreducible character $g$ were missing, it would be perpendicular to every $\chi_m$. The continuous function $g(\alpha)\sin\alpha$ would be perpendicular to every sine on $[0,\pi]$. Its odd extension to $[-\pi,\pi]$ is continuous and periodic, because its endpoint values are zero. Every Fourier coefficient vanishes: sine coefficients by the orthogonality just stated and cosine coefficients by oddness. The circle case of Peter--Weyl makes that function zero in $L^2$, hence everywhere by continuity. Thus $g=0$ on $(0,\pi)$ and, by continuity, at the endpoints too. An irreducible character has norm $1$, a contradiction. No irreducible is missing.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:catalanu2}
\idea The Vandermonde factor inserts a sine square, making the difference of two Wallis integrals.
\writeup The integrand depends only on $\varphi=\theta_1-\theta_2$. Periodicity reduces the normalized two-torus integral to a normalized circle integral. With $x=\varphi/2$, Weyl's factor $1/2!$ gives
\[
\mathbb E|\operatorname{tr}U|^{2a}
=\frac{2\cdot4^a}\pi\int_0^\pi\cos^{2a}x(1-\cos^2x)\,\dd x.
\]
Let $I_a=\int_0^\pi\cos^{2a}x\,\dd x=\pi4^{-a}\binom{2a}{a}$, the Wallis integral already established in Volume~1's integration chapter. Substitution yields
\[
\frac{2\cdot4^a}\pi(I_a-I_{a+1})
=2\binom{2a}{a}-\frac12\binom{2a+2}{a+1}
=\frac1{a+1}\binom{2a}{a}.
\]
The last equality uses $\binom{2a+2}{a+1}=2(2a+1)\binom{2a}{a}/(a+1)$. It also works for $a=0$, giving $1$. Theorem~\ref{thm:traces} identifies the integral with the desired permutation count. This is the Catalan number $C_a$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:domino}
\idea Raising an alternant exponent by two can cross at most one distinct integer exponent without either stopping or colliding. That crossing accounts for the negative sign.
\writeup Put $l=\lambda+\delta$, so $l_1>\cdots>l_n$, and expand
$p_2a_l=\sum_i a_{l+2e_i}$.
For $i=1$, or when $l_{i-1}\ge l_i+3$, the raised vector is still decreasing. It contributes $s_{\lambda+2e_i}$ after division by $a_\delta$: a horizontal domino with positive sign.

If $l_{i-1}=l_i+2$, two entries coincide and the determinant is zero. If $l_{i-1}=l_i+1$, the raised entry crosses the previous one. Swapping them introduces a minus sign. When $i\ge3$ and $l_{i-2}=l_i+2$, there is a new collision, so again the determinant is zero. Otherwise the reordered vector is strictly decreasing; the weight has increased by $1$ in each of rows $i-1,i$. The condition $l_{i-1}=l_i+1$ means those rows had equal lengths. The absence of the second collision is exactly the condition that their vertical addition leaves a diagram.

Every legal horizontal or vertical domino determines its unique raised index $i$, so no term is lost or counted twice. This proves the signed sum on distinct coordinates; polynomial continuation covers repeated coordinates. Shifting all entries of $\lambda$ multiplies every term by the same determinant power and leaves the argument unchanged.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch11-statistic}
\idea Traces are Fourier modes of the eigenvalue count. Distinct signed frequencies are perpendicular, though their variances depend on the matrix size.
\writeup Set $p_k=\sum_jt_j^k$ for $k\ne0$. Then
$L_f=nc_0+\sum_{k\ne0}c_kp_k$ and $\mathbb E p_k=0$, also for negative $k$ by conjugation. For signed nonzero integers $k,l$, rotational invariance gives
$\mathbb E[p_k\overline{p_l}]=0$ if $k\ne l$.
For $k=l$, Proposition~\ref{prop:powertraces} and conjugation give $\mathbb E|p_k|^2=\min(|k|,n)$. Therefore
\[
\mathbb E L_f=nc_0,\qquad
\mathbb E|L_f-nc_0|^2=\sum_{k\ne0}\min(|k|,n)|c_k|^2.
\]
For independent uniform points, orthogonality of circle monomials instead gives $n\sum_{k\ne0}|c_k|^2$.

For $\cos\theta+2\cos2\theta$, the coefficients at $\pm1$ are $1/2$ and at $\pm2$ are $1$. The mean is zero and the unitary variance is $1/2+2\min(2,n)$: it is $5/2$ at $n=1$ and $9/2$ for $n\ge2$. The independent variance is $5n/2$. A constant polynomial has both variances zero, as the formula predicts.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch11-detmoment}
\idea A central rotation records the total weight. Orthogonality then extracts the determinant's coefficient.
\writeup Replacing $U$ by $zU$ multiplies the integrand by $z^{nr+a-b}$. If this integer is nonzero, choose $z$ on the circle with that power different from $1$. Equality of the two expectations forces the expectation to vanish. For the converse, first take $r\ge0$ and $b=a+nr$. Twisting by $\det^r$ adds $r$ to every entry of a weight. Expand both trace powers in characters using Theorem~\ref{thm:traces}. Orthogonality gives the finite sum
\[
\sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash a\\\ell(\lambda)\le n}}
f^\lambda f^{\lambda+(r^n)}.
\]
Here $\lambda$ is padded to $n$ rows, and the shifted diagram has $b$ boxes. Every summand is a positive integer: every finite partition diagram has a standard tableau, for example the row-by-row filling. There is at least one $\lambda$, including the empty diagram when $a=0$. Thus the expectation is positive. For $r<0$, take the complex conjugate and interchange $a,b$; this reduces to the case just proved. In this family the balance condition is both necessary and sufficient.

For the requested value, $\det$ is $\chi_{(1^n)}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:traces} expands $p_1^n$ in characters, and its coefficient at this weight is $f^{(1^n)}=1$: a column has just one standard filling. Character orthogonality gives
$\mathbb E[\overline{\det U}(\operatorname{tr}U)^n]=1$.
\end{solution}

\begin{solution}{ex:v10new-ch11-projective}
\idea A quotient representation exists exactly when the subgroup being collapsed acts trivially.
\writeup Let $s=\sum_j\lambda_j$. Every monomial of $s_\lambda$ has total degree $s$, because the numerator and denominator alternants have degrees differing by $s$. Hence
$\chi_\lambda(zI)=z^s\dim V_\lambda$.
The central operator $\rho(zI)$ is scalar by Schur's lemma, so this trace equality makes it $z^s I$. It equals $I$ for every unit complex $z$ exactly when $s=0$.

If this holds, define the quotient representation by $[U]\mapsto\rho(U)$. It is well defined and continuous by the definition of the quotient topology. Conversely any quotient representation must kill every $zI$, proving the criterion. The determinant twist changes the sum to $|\mu|+nr$. An integer $r$ exists exactly when $n$ divides $|\mu|$, and it is uniquely $-|\mu|/n$. For $n\ge2$, the standard weight has sum $1$ and does not descend. The trace-zero conjugation weight $(1,0,\ldots,0,-1)$ has sum zero and does descend. For $n=1$, the quotient is trivial, consistent with the zero-weight condition.
\end{solution}
cross_volume_reference_lines: For a finite group, averaging means adding a function over the group and dividing by its order. For a circle, it means integrating once around the circumference. Haar measure lets us do the same thing on a compact group. Once that average is available, the arguments about finite-group representations from Volume~3 have room to work again.

Throughout the chapter, $G$ is a compact matrix Lie group: a closed, compact subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_N(\C)$. The examples to keep in mind are $U(n)$, $SU(n)$ and $SO(n)$. Its Haar probability measure $\mu$ is invariant under multiplication on either side; Volume~9, Theorem~8.3 and Corollary~8.2 establish this. A representation means a continuous homomorphism $\rho\colon G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space. The zero representation is allowed; an irreducible representation is nonzero. When $U(n)$ appears, $n$ is a positive integer.

Schur's lemma from Volume~3 applies without a finiteness assumption on the group: its proof concerns invariant subspaces and eigenvalues of a linear map on a finite-dimensional complex space. Averaging a linear map will turn it into just such an intertwining map.

For $U(1)$, every irreducible is $z\mapsto z^k$, $k\in\Z$. Indeed, the commuting unitary matrices of a representation have a common eigenbasis, so an irreducible has dimension one; Volume~8, Theorem~13.11 classifies the continuous circle characters. Orthogonality becomes

It also separates points. Two different matrices in $G\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_N(\C)$ differ in some entry. That entry is a coefficient of the defining representation on $\C^N$. The complex Stone--Weierstrass theorem, Volume~7, Theorem~4.19(b), now gives (a). The matrix-group assumption is exactly what made separation immediate.

Completed-measure sets differ from Borel sets only by null sets, so they cause no extra difficulty. Simple functions are dense in $L^2$ by Volume~7's integration theory. Approximating their indicators proves that $C(G)$ is dense too.

Insert these coefficients into the Hilbert-space expansion and Parseval identity of Volume~8. Grouping the $d_\rho^2$ terms for each $\rho$ gives the trace formulas in (b). The order of the indices explains why the Fourier transform uses $\rho(g)^*$.
